Chapter 2 Stress and equilibrium

2.10 Mathematics: the determinant

In section 2.9 we wrote the stress at a point as a matrix \(\ten\sigma\) whose rows are the traction vectors \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\), \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \(\vek t(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}})\), and Cauchy's formula as \(\vek t(\vek n) = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) ((2.54)). A question from section 2.6.6 is still open: on which face through a point is the normal stress largest? In pure shear we found faces there on which the traction vector points exactly along the normal. The cube was loaded only by forces along its faces, of size \(\tau_0\) per unit area, and the stress matrix had the rows \((0, 0, \tau_0)\), \((0, 0, 0)\) and \((\tau_0, 0, 0)\). On the face perpendicular to the diagonal \(AC\) of the cube, with the normal \(\vek n\)\( = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\), we had \(\vek t(\vek n) = \tau_0\,\vek n\), that is, \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = \tau_0\,\vek n\). The identity matrix does not change a vector, \(\mat I\,\vek n = \vek n\) (lemma 1.109), so we can write this equality as

\[(\ten\sigma - \tau_0\,\mat I)\,\vek n = \vek 0 .\]

So the matrix \(\ten\sigma - \tau_0\,\mat I\) sends the nonzero vector \(\vek n\) to the zero vector. In section 2.11 we will look for such faces for every stress matrix. For this we need a test that tells, from the nine entries of a matrix, whether the matrix sends some nonzero vector to the zero vector.

The same test answers the question from section 1.16 of when a matrix has an inverse matrix. A matrix that sends a nonzero vector to the zero vector has none. If \(\mat B\) were the inverse matrix of \(\mat M = \ten\sigma - \tau_0\,\mat I\), then by item 1 of lemma 1.100 on the properties of the matrix product we would have \(\vek n = \mat I\,\vek n = (\mat B\mat M)\,\vek n = \mat B\,(\mat M\vek n) = \mat B\,\vek 0 = \vek 0\), but we know that \(\vek n\) is not the zero vector.

A third question was left open in chapter 1. In section 1.17 we said that for small strains the volume of a small piece of a body changes, relative to itself, by about \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and we saved the exact relation for this chapter.

From history

The question of when several equations have a common solution is older than matrices. Already before 1683 Seki Kowa in Japan treated \(n\) equations and knew how to form an expression from their coefficients that must be zero for the equations to have a common solution. He knew that this expression, when expanded, has \(n!\) terms and that rows and columns are interchangeable (CAJORI, PDF p. 96).

Why so many terms, we see on a table of coefficients of size \(3 \times 3\). Each term is a product of one coefficient from each row and each column. For the first row we have \(n\) choices of column, for the second the \(n - 1\) remaining ones, for the third one when \(n = 3\), in all \(n \cdot (n - 1) \cdots 1 = n!\) choices. Rows and columns appear in the terms on equal terms. That the signs agree as well we show for \(n = 3\) in item 6 of lemma 2.73.

On 28 April 1693 Leibniz argued in a letter to the Marquis Guillaume de l'Hôpital that numbers in long calculations can be as useful as letters. For letters do not tell how the quantities they denote are related to each other, whereas numbers do (MUIR, PDF p. 24-25). He showed three equations in two unknowns from which he wanted to eliminate both unknowns by one general rule. He labelled the coefficients with two numbers, the first telling in which equation a coefficient stands and the second beside which unknown (MUIR, PDF p. 24-25). If we treat the number \(1\) as a third unknown, these are three equations in three unknowns with zero right-hand side. His question is therefore our question of when a \(3 \times 3\) matrix sends the nonzero vector \((1, x, y)\) to the zero vector. In the elimination he noticed a regularity and derived from it a rule for which products of coefficients appear in the result and with what sign. The rule held for any number of equations and unknowns (MUIR, PDF p. 26). The letter was published only in 1850 and did not influence later development (MUIR, PDF p. 27).

Gabriel Cramer came to a similar rule in 1750 from a geometric question.

A curve of the second degree (krivulja druge stopnje) is a curve whose equation contains, besides the coordinates themselves, also their squares and the product \(xy\), like an ellipse. Such an equation has six coefficients, but it does not change if we multiply it by the same number, so only five are independent. Each point through which the curve passes gives one equation for these coefficients, so the curve is determined by five points (MUIR, PDF p. 30), if no four of them lie on one line.

Why this condition? Take four points on the \(x\) axis, \((0, 0)\), \((1, 0)\), \((2, 0)\) and \((3, 0)\), and a fifth point \((0, 1)\). On the \(x\) axis we have \(y = 0\), and the equation of the curve \(A x^2 + B xy + C y^2 + D x + E y + F = 0\) from figure 2.199 shrinks there to \(A x^2 + D x + F = 0\). This equation has four solutions only if \(A = D = F = 0\), since otherwise it has at most two. What remains is \(y\,(B x + C y + E) = 0\), that is the \(x\) axis together with the line \(B x + C y + E = 0\), which must pass through the fifth point. There are infinitely many such lines, three are drawn, \(y = 1\), \(y = x + 1\) and \(x + 4y = 4\), and each gives a curve of the second degree through all five points. The five equations for the coefficients are dependent here (rank \(4\), computed with SymPy), so they do not determine the curve.

Because the calculation for five points is long, Cramer published in an appendix to his book on algebraic curves a general rule for solving \(n\) equations in \(n\) unknowns (MUIR, PDF p. 29-31). His rule spread and was taught in schools for many years, while Leibniz's stayed hidden (MUIR, PDF p. 32).

On 12 January 1771 Alexandre-Théophile Vandermonde read to the Paris Academy a memoir on elimination (MUIR, PDF pp. 35-36). He labelled the coefficients by their place in the table, as Leibniz did, and wrote that the sign of the expression reverses if two indices in it are interchanged (MUIR, PDF p. 40). He was the first to give a connected and logical exposition of the theory of these expressions (CAJORI, PDF p. 282, MUIR, PDF p. 42). In 1772 Pierre-Simon Laplace called the expression that arises in elimination a resultant (resultanta) (MUIR, PDF p. 42 and 43). Thus arose an expression in the coefficients of equations, built by a definite rule, which must be zero for the equations to have a common solution.

All three questions, that is whether a matrix sends a nonzero vector to the zero vector, whether it has an inverse matrix and how the volume of a small piece of a body changes, are answered by one number computed from the nine entries of a matrix. We shall reach this number geometrically.

A matrix sends the cube with the edges \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) to a body whose faces are parallelograms, and this number is the volume of that body, equipped with a sign. If it is zero, the body is flattened into a plane, and then the matrix sends some direction to zero. The route is this. First we compute the volume of such a body with the scalar and the vector product. Then we define this number for every matrix, prove its rules of calculation and the rule for getting it for the product of two matrices. With them we show when a matrix sends a nonzero vector to zero and when it has an inverse matrix. Finally we compute how the volume of a small piece of a body changes.

In this section all vectors are written with components in the same right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, of the kind we needed for the vector product in section 2.8. The matrices are \(3 \times 3\), in a few places \(2 \times 2\), and we label their rows and columns with \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), as for the components of vectors. When we multiply a matrix by a vector, we write the vector as a column.

2.10.1 The volume of a parallelepiped

Let us begin in the plane. In section 2.8 we saw that the length of the vector product \(|\vek b\times\vek c|\) is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the vectors \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) drawn from the same point. We computed the vector product with components,

\[\vek b\times\vek c = (b_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{z}} - b_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{y}},\ b_{\mathrm{z}} c_{\mathrm{x}} - b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{z}},\ b_{\mathrm{x}} c_{\mathrm{y}} - b_{\mathrm{y}} c_{\mathrm{x}}) .\]

Now let us add a third vector. The vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\), drawn from the same point \(P\), span a parallelepiped (paralelepiped). It is the body made of all points \(P + s\,\vek a + t\,\vek b + w\,\vek c\) for which the numbers \(s\), \(t\) and \(w\) lie between \(0\) and \(1\) (figure 2.202). Its faces are six parallelograms, in pairs of parallel ones. The parallelogram of the vectors \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\), the face at \(s = 0\), is called the base (osnovna ploskev). The opposite face at \(s = 1\) is the base moved by the vector \(\vek a\). The box of section 2.7 is a parallelepiped with mutually perpendicular edges. The sheared cube of section 1.6.2 also became a parallelepiped after the push, since each of its faces became a parallelogram.

We know its volume from school. It is the area of the base times the height, and the height is the distance between the plane of the base and the plane of the opposite face, measured perpendicular to the base. In the same way, in lemma 2.24 on the faces and volume of the tetrahedron, we took the formula for the volume of a pyramid from school.

How do we compute the height with vectors? We need a direction perpendicular to the base. The vector product \(\vek b\times\vek c\) is perpendicular to \(\vek b\) and to \(\vek c\) (item 4 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product). So it is also perpendicular to every vector \(t\,\vek b + w\,\vek c\) between two points of the base, since by the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12)

\[(\vek b\times\vek c)\cdot(t\,\vek b + w\,\vek c) = t\,(\vek b\times\vek c)\cdot\vek b + w\,(\vek b\times\vek c)\cdot\vek c = t \cdot 0 + w \cdot 0 = 0 .\]

If \(\vek b\times\vek c\) is not the zero vector, then \(\vek n = (\vek b\times\vek c)/|\vek b\times\vek c|\) is the unit vector in its direction (lemma 1.19), so it is the unit normal of the base. We split the edge \(\vek a\) into a part in the direction of \(\vek n\) and a part perpendicular to \(\vek n\) (lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector):

\[\vek a = (\vek a\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n + \big(\vek a - (\vek a\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n\big) .\]

In figure 2.202 the first part is the blue vertical arrow and the second the blue dashed arrow. The second part is perpendicular to the normal, so it is parallel to the base, and when we move along it we do not move away from the plane of the base. We move away from it only by the first part. So the height is its length, \(|\vek a\cdot\vek n|\), the absolute value of the projection of the edge \(\vek a\) onto the normal (definition 2.13). We take the absolute value because the projection is negative when \(\vek a\) points to the other side of the base than \(\vek n\). The area of the base times the height is

\[|\vek b\times\vek c|\,\Big|\vek a\cdot\frac{\vek b\times\vek c}{|\vek b\times\vek c|}\Big| = |\vek b\times\vek c|\,\frac{|\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)|}{|\vek b\times\vek c|} = |\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)| ,\]

where we took out the positive number \(1/|\vek b\times\vek c|\) by item 3 of the properties of the scalar product. The length \(|\vek b\times\vek c|\) cancels, and what remains is a number computed from the components of all three vectors with both products. The number gets a name.

Definition 2.68 Scalar triple product (mešani produkt)

The scalar triple product (mešani produkt) of the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\), written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, is the number \(\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.3 (10*) (PDF p. 399), CM §2.2.2.3 (PDF p. 45).

The name says that it involves three vectors and gives a number, a scalar, because the last product taken is the scalar product. KREYSZIG also calls it the mixed product, since both products appear in it, and writes it \((\vek a\ \vek b\ \vek c)\), while CM writes \([\mathbf{ABC}]\) (KREYSZIG §9.3 (10), PDF p. 399, CM (2.2.20), PDF p. 45). We will simply write it with the dot and the cross. Let us state the computation above as a claim.

Lemma 2.69 Volume of a parallelepiped (prostornina paralelepipeda)

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\), written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, is \(|\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)|\).

Proof

We compute the volume as the area of the base times the height and express both numbers with the two products.

  1. From school we take that the volume of a parallelepiped is the area of the base times the height, the distance between the plane of the base and the plane of the opposite face. The base is the parallelogram of the vectors \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\). Its area is \(|\vek b\times\vek c|\) (section 2.8).
  2. If \(\vek b\times\vek c = \vek 0\), the vectors \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) lie on one line, the area of the base is zero, the parallelepiped is flattened, and its volume is zero. Also \(\vek a\cdot\vek 0 = 0\), so the claim holds.
  3. Let \(\vek b\times\vek c \neq \vek 0\). The vector \(\vek b\times\vek c\) is perpendicular to \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) (item 4 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product), so \(\vek n = (\vek b\times\vek c)/|\vek b\times\vek c|\) is a unit vector perpendicular to the base (lemma 1.19).
  4. By lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector, \(\vek a = (\vek a\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n + \vek r\), where \(\vek r\) is perpendicular to \(\vek n\). From school we take that a vector perpendicular to the normal of a plane is parallel to the plane. When we move from \(P\) by \(\vek a\), we therefore move away from the plane of the base only by the length of the part \((\vek a\cdot\vek n)\,\vek n\). The height is \(|\vek a\cdot\vek n|\).
  5. By item 3 of the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12), \(\vek a\cdot\vek n = \vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)/|\vek b\times\vek c|\).
  6. The volume is \(|\vek b\times\vek c| \cdot |\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)|/|\vek b\times\vek c| = |\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)|\).

Source: KREYSZIG §9.3, Theorem 2(b) (PDF pp. 399-400), which proves the claim with the same idea, as the height \(|\vek a|\,|\cos\gamma|\) times the area of the base, where \(\gamma\) is the angle between \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\times\vek c\). CM §2.2.2.3, Fig. 2.2.5 (PDF p. 45), states the claim with a figure. The steps with the projection onto the normal are not from the sources.

Let us test it on the parallelepiped of figure 2.202, with the edges \(\vek a = (1, 1, 2)\), \(\vek b = (2, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek c = (1, 3, 0)\). First,

\[\vek b\times\vek c = (0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 3,\ 0 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 0,\ 2 \cdot 3 - 0 \cdot 1) = (0, 0, 6) ,\]

and then \(\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c) = 1 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 6 = 12\). Let us check it the school way. The vectors \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) have the component \(z\) equal to zero, so the base lies in the plane \(z = 0\). It is a parallelogram with the base side \(2\) along the axis \(x\) and the height \(3\), the component \(y\) of the vector \(\vek c\), so its area is \(2 \cdot 3 = 6\), which is the length of the vector \((0, 0, 6)\). The normal is \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and the height of the parallelepiped is \(\vek a\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = 2\), the component \(z\) of the edge \(\vek a\). The volume is \(6 \cdot 2 = 12\). The components \(x\) and \(y\) of the edge \(\vek a\) make up the part parallel to the base, which does not take us away from it, so they do not count here.

What happens if we tilt the edge \(\vek a\) differently? In figure 2.204, on the left is the parallelepiped with the edge \(\vek a = (1, 1, 2)\) of figure 2.202, and on the right the parallelepiped with the edge \(\vek a = (2, -1, 2)\), which leans further to the right and towards us. Both stand on the same base, the parallelogram of the vectors \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) with area \(6\). In both we split the edge \(\vek a\) as in figure 2.202. The part parallel to the base is \((1, 1, 0)\) on the left and \((2, -1, 0)\) on the right. Both parts are drawn from the top of the height to the tip of the edge \(\vek a\), in the plane \(z = 2\) of the opposite face. The part in the direction of the normal is \((0, 0, 2)\) in both, so the height is \(2\) in both and the volume is \(6 \cdot 2 = 12\) in both. The scalar triple product gives the same, \((2, -1, 2)\cdot(0, 0, 6) = 0 + 0 + 12 = 12\). The tilt changes the shape of the body but not its volume, as long as the base and the height stay the same.

The scalar triple product tells us one more thing that the volume loses, a sign. Since \(\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c) = |\vek b\times\vek c|\,(\vek a\cdot\vek n)\), it has the sign of the projection \(\vek a\cdot\vek n\). The base face lies in a plane, and \(\vek b\times\vek c\) stands perpendicular to it. The scalar triple product is positive when the edge \(\vek a\) points to the same side of the base as the vector \(\vek b\times\vek c\), and negative when it points to the other side. This is exactly what we need for the test promised in section 2.8. There, following KREYSZIG, we called a triple of vectors right-handed when, in this order, it points like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand. The right-hand rule describes a position in space and does not calculate with components, so we cannot prove it with numbers, but we can check it with numbers. For the unit vectors of the axes, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 0) = (1, 0, 0) = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so

\[\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = 1 > 0 ,\]

and the triple \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is right-handed, because our coordinate system is. The order of the vectors counts. Since \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (0 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1,\ 1 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 0) = (0, -1, 0)\), we get \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\cdot(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = -1 < 0\), and the triple \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) points like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the left hand. CM therefore takes the sign of the scalar triple product as the test: it calls a triple whose scalar triple product is greater than zero positively oriented (CM, PDF p. 126). We do the same and replace the right-hand rule by the sign of the scalar triple product.

Definition 2.70 Orientation of a triple (orientacija trojice)

A triple of vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) in this order, written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, is right-handed (desnosučna) when its scalar triple product is positive, \(\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c) > 0\), and left-handed (levosučna) when it is negative, \(\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c) < 0\). Whether a triple is right-handed or left-handed is called its orientation (orientacija). A triple whose scalar triple product is zero, whose parallelepiped is flattened, has no orientation.

Source: CM (PDF p. 126), KREYSZIG §9.3 (PDF p. 395). KREYSZIG describes a right-handed triple by the right-hand rule, and CM calls a triple with a positive scalar triple product positively oriented.

A left-handed triple looks like the mirror image of a right-handed one, like a left hand in a mirror held in front of a right hand (figure 2.206). Let us check this on the unit vectors of the axes. A mirror in the plane of the axes \(y\) and \(z\) changes the sign of the components \(x\) and leaves the other components. The triple \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is mirrored into the triple \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and \((-\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})\cdot(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = -1\). The mirror image of the triple \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is left-handed.

The definition must also say which triple has no orientation. Let us take the vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and a third vector \(\vek c = (1, 1, 0)\), which lies in the same plane \(z = 0\). The triple \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek c\) has no orientation if its scalar triple product is neither positive nor negative, that is, if it is zero.

  1. The vector product of the last two vectors is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek c = (1 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1,\ 0 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0,\ 0 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 1) = (0, 0, -1)\).
  2. The scalar triple product is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(0, 0, -1) = 1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot (-1) = 0\). All three vectors lie in the plane \(z = 0\), the parallelepiped is flattened and has no volume.
  3. The scalar triple product is neither positive nor negative, so the triple has no orientation.

If we raise the third vector only a little, an orientation appears. For \(\vek c = (1, 1, 0{,}1)\) we have \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek c = (0{,}1;\ 0;\ -1)\) and the scalar triple product is \(0{,}1 > 0\), the triple is right-handed. For \(\vek c = (1, 1, -0{,}1)\) we have \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek c = (-0{,}1;\ 0;\ -1)\) and the scalar triple product is \(-0{,}1 < 0\), the triple is left-handed. The sign changes exactly at \(z = 0\), where the scalar triple product vanishes.

Now we can write with numbers the right-hand rule for the vector product, which in section 2.8 we checked only for the unit vectors of the axes, and prove its numerical form for any two vectors whose vector product is not the zero vector. The statement that the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek a\times\vek b\), in this order, point like the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger of the right hand means, by definition 2.70 of the orientation of a triple, that the scalar triple product of this triple is positive.

Lemma 2.71 Direction of the vector product (smer vektorskega produkta)

Let \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) be vectors written in a chosen right-handed rectangular Cartesian coordinate system, and let \(\vek a\times\vek b \neq \vek 0\). Then the triple \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek a\times\vek b\) is right-handed, since

\[\vek a\cdot\big(\vek b\times(\vek a\times\vek b)\big) = |\vek a\times\vek b|^2 > 0 . \tag{2.69}\]
Proof

We must show that the scalar triple product of the triple equals \(|\vek a\times\vek b|^2\). First we show with components that the scalar triple product does not change when we move the last vector to the first place.

  1. Let \(\vek u\), \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) be any vectors. By (2.39) and (2.6),
    \[\vek u\cdot(\vek v\times\vek w) = u_{\mathrm{x}} (v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}} - v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}}) + u_{\mathrm{y}} (v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}} - v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}}) + u_{\mathrm{z}} (v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}} - v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}}) .\]
    Removing the brackets gives six terms, \(u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(-u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  2. In the same way,
    \[\vek w\cdot(\vek u\times\vek v) = w_{\mathrm{x}} (u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}} - u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}}) + w_{\mathrm{y}} (u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}} - u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}}) + w_{\mathrm{z}} (u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} - u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}}) ,\]
    which is the six terms \(w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(-w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  3. In a product of numbers the order of the factors does not matter. So the term \(w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}}\) of step 2 is the term \(u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}}\) of step 1, the term \(-w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}}\) is \(-u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}}\), the term \(w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}}\) is \(u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\), the term \(-w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}}\) is \(-u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}}\), the term \(w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}}\) is \(u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the term \(-w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}}\) is \(-u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\). Both sums have the same terms with the same signs, so \(\vek u\cdot(\vek v\times\vek w) = \vek w\cdot(\vek u\times\vek v)\).
  4. We insert \(\vek u = \vek a\), \(\vek v = \vek b\) and \(\vek w = \vek a\times\vek b\). By step 3, \(\vek a\cdot\big(\vek b\times(\vek a\times\vek b)\big) = (\vek a\times\vek b)\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b)\).
  5. By item 4 of the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12) this number is \(|\vek a\times\vek b|^2\). It is positive, since \(\vek a\times\vek b\) is not the zero vector. By definition 2.70 of orientation the triple \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek a\times\vek b\) is therefore a right-handed triple.

Source: KREYSZIG §9.3 (PDF p. 394) and CM (PDF p. 43) take the fact that the triple \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek a\times\vek b\) points like the right hand as part of the definition of the vector product. The proof is not from the sources.

Let us test it on the fly's flight \(\vek a = (1, 2, -2)\) and the vector \(\vek b = (2, -1, 0)\) from section 2.8.1, for which \(\vek a\times\vek b = (-2, -4, -5)\). By (2.39),

\[\begin{aligned} \vek b\times(\vek a\times\vek b) &= (2, -1, 0)\times(-2, -4, -5) \\ &= \big((-1)(-5) - 0 \cdot (-4),\ \ 0 \cdot (-2) - 2 \cdot (-5),\ \ 2 \cdot (-4) - (-1)(-2)\big) \\ &= (5, 10, -10) , \end{aligned}\]

and the scalar triple product is \(1 \cdot 5 + 2 \cdot 10 + (-2)(-10) = 45\), which is \(|\vek a\times\vek b|^2 = 4 + 16 + 25\). The vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) span a plane, and \(\vek a\times\vek b\) stands perpendicular to it. This does not yet fix the orientation, since the opposite vector \(-(\vek a\times\vek b)\) would also stand perpendicular to it. The sign fixes it. The scalar triple product is positive, \(45 > 0\), so by definition 2.70 the triple is right-handed. We will need the exchange of order from steps 1 to 3 of the proof, which holds for all vectors \(\vek u\), \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\), in the next section too.

2.10.2 The determinant of a matrix

Now to matrices. What does a \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\) do with the unit cube (enotska kocka), the cube with the edges \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the origin? By (1.39) the component \(i\) of the vector \(\mat A\vek v\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}} v_{\mathrm{j}}\), where the indices \(i\) and \(j\) run over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). For \(\vek v = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 0)\) all factors \(v_{\mathrm{j}}\) in the sum are zero except \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\), so only the term with \(j = x\) remains:

\[(\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{i}} = A_{\mathrm{ix}} .\]

So the components of the vector \(\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) are \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{yx}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{zx}}\), the entries of the column \(x\) of the matrix. In the same way \(\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) is the column \(y\) and \(\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) the column \(z\). We call the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\). A point of the cube \(s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + w\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) with the numbers \(s\), \(t\), \(w\) between \(0\) and \(1\) goes, by the linearity of the product with a matrix (lemma 1.98), to the point

\[\mat A\,(s\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + t\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + w\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = s\,\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + t\,\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + w\,\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = s\,\vek a + t\,\vek b + w\,\vek c .\]

So the matrix sends the unit cube, which has the volume \(1\), to the parallelepiped spanned by its columns (figure 2.210). The scalar triple product of the columns tells how many times larger the volume of this parallelepiped is than that of the cube, and whether the triple \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) has the same orientation as \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Definition 2.72 Determinant (determinanta)

Let \(\mat A\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with the columns \(\vek a = (A_{\mathrm{xx}}, A_{\mathrm{yx}}, A_{\mathrm{zx}})\), \(\vek b = (A_{\mathrm{xy}}, A_{\mathrm{yy}}, A_{\mathrm{zy}})\) and \(\vek c = (A_{\mathrm{xz}}, A_{\mathrm{yz}}, A_{\mathrm{zz}})\). The determinant (determinanta) of the matrix \(\mat A\) is the number \(\det\mat A = \vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)\), that is, the volume of the parallelepiped with a sign. With the entries of the matrix it reads

\[\begin{aligned} \det\mat A &= A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}} + A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}} A_{\mathrm{zx}} + A_{\mathrm{xz}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{zy}} \\ &\quad - A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yz}} A_{\mathrm{zy}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{zz}} - A_{\mathrm{xz}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{zx}} . \end{aligned} \tag{2.70}\]

The determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix with the entries \(A_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{yx}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is the number \(\det\mat A = A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}}\).

Source: CM (2.3.9) (PDF p. 66), KREYSZIG §9.3 (10) (PDF p. 399) and §7.6 (1), (4) (PDF pp. 317-318).

We get the formula (2.70) from the scalar triple product of the columns in three steps.

  1. Into the formula for the vector product we insert the components of the columns \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\):
    \[\vek b\times\vek c = \big(A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}} - A_{\mathrm{zy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}},\ A_{\mathrm{zy}} A_{\mathrm{xz}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}},\ A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}} - A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{xz}}\big) .\]
  2. We compute the scalar product with the column \(\vek a = (A_{\mathrm{xx}}, A_{\mathrm{yx}}, A_{\mathrm{zx}})\) by (2.6):
    \[\begin{aligned} \det\mat A &= A_{\mathrm{xx}}\,(A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}} - A_{\mathrm{zy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}}) \\ &\quad + A_{\mathrm{yx}}\,(A_{\mathrm{zy}} A_{\mathrm{xz}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}}) \\ &\quad + A_{\mathrm{zx}}\,(A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}} - A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{xz}}) . \end{aligned} \tag{2.71}\]
  3. We remove the brackets and rearrange the six terms so that the three with a plus come first. In each term we order the factors by rows, first the entry from the row \(x\), then from \(y\) and last from \(z\). We get (2.70).

There is a pattern in the formula worth noticing (figure 2.211). Each of the six terms is a product of three entries, one from each row and one from each column. There are exactly six such choices: the entry from the row \(x\) can be taken from three columns, the entry from the row \(y\) from the two remaining ones, and the entry from the row \(z\) from the last one left, and \(3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 6\). Three choices come with a plus, three with a minus. A term with a plus is for example \(A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}}\), the product of the entries on the main diagonal. If in each term we write down in order the columns of the entries from the rows \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), the terms with a plus give the sequences \(xyz\), \(yzx\) and \(zxy\), which follow the cycle \(x \to y \to z \to x\) and only start at another letter, and the terms with a minus give \(xzy\), \(yxz\) and \(zyx\), in which two letters of the sequence \(xyz\) are exchanged. That exchanging two columns reverses the sign of the determinant, we will prove in the lemma below. The formula (2.71), called the expansion by the first column (razvoj po prvem stolpcu), tells how the determinant is easiest to compute: each entry of the first column is multiplied by the determinant of the \(2 \times 2\) matrix that remains when we cross out its row and its column, and the signs alternate, \(+\), \(-\), \(+\) (KREYSZIG §7.6 (4), PDF p. 318). For the entry \(A_{\mathrm{yx}}\) this determinant is \(A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}} - A_{\mathrm{xz}} A_{\mathrm{zy}}\), and the bracket in (2.71) is its negative.

Let us test it on the matrix of figure 2.210. Its columns are the edges of the parallelepiped of figure 2.202:

\[\mat A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

By (2.70),

\[\det\mat A = 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 0 \cdot 2 = 12 ,\]

as we computed above with the scalar triple product. The matrix sends the unit cube to a parallelepiped with twelve times the volume, and the triple of its columns is right-handed. For the identity matrix the columns are \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and \(\det\mat I = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = 1\). The identity matrix does not change the cube.

And the determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix? Such a matrix sends vectors of the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) to vectors of the same plane. Let us put it into a \(3 \times 3\) matrix that has zeros in the row \(z\) and the column \(z\), except for the number \(1\) at the place \(zz\). By (2.70) this larger matrix has the determinant

\[\begin{aligned} &A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} \cdot 1 + A_{\mathrm{xy}} \cdot 0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot A_{\mathrm{yx}} \cdot 0 \\ &\quad - A_{\mathrm{xx}} \cdot 0 \cdot 0 - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot A_{\mathrm{yy}} \cdot 0 = A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} - A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} , \end{aligned}\]

which is exactly the determinant of the \(2 \times 2\) matrix. The columns \((A_{\mathrm{xx}}, A_{\mathrm{yx}}, 0)\) and \((A_{\mathrm{xy}}, A_{\mathrm{yy}}, 0)\) of the larger matrix lie in the plane \(z = 0\), and the third column is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The right side of figure 2.212 shows this for the matrix with the columns \((3, 1)\) and \((1, 2)\): the columns of the larger matrix are \((3, 1, 0)\) and \((1, 2, 0)\), and the third is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). So the parallelepiped has the parallelogram of the two columns in the plane as its base. The edge \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) is perpendicular to the plane \(z = 0\) and has the length \(1\), so the height of the parallelepiped is \(1\), and its volume is the area of the base times \(1\). The absolute value of the determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix is therefore the area of the parallelogram spanned by its two columns (left in the same figure). We got the same number in section 2.8 as the length of the vector product of two vectors in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The matrix with the columns \((3, 1)\) and \((1, 2)\) has the determinant \(3 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 1 = 5\), and it sends the unit square with the area \(1\) to a parallelogram with the area \(5\).

The determinant exists for every square matrix, that is, for every matrix with as many rows as columns, of size \(n \times n\). CM and KREYSZIG define it by an expansion by a row or a column, which expresses a determinant of size \(n\) by determinants of size \(n - 1\) (CM (2.3.7), PDF p. 65, KREYSZIG §7.7 (3a), PDF p. 320). For \(n = 3\) this definition gives the formula (2.70), for \(n = 2\) our formula for the \(2 \times 2\) matrix. The absolute value of the determinant is an area for \(n = 2\), a volume for \(n = 3\), and for larger \(n\) a volume in a space with \(n\) dimensions. We will need only \(2 \times 2\) and \(3 \times 3\) matrices. CM also writes the determinant as \(|A|\) (CM, PDF p. 65). A matrix that is not square has no determinant.

From history

The word determinant (determinanta) was first used by Gauss in 1801 in his book Disquisitiones arithmeticae. He gave this name to the number \(b^2 - ac\), on which, as he wrote, the properties of the expression \(a x^2 + 2 b x y + c y^2\) depend (MUIR, PDF p. 81 and 82). Up to the sign this number is the determinant of the matrix with the columns \((a, b)\) and \((b, c)\). Cauchy introduced the name in 1812 for the general expressions that we call determinants today (CAJORI, PDF p. 356, MUIR, PDF p. 110 and 111). We meet his paper of that year in section 2.10.3. The two upright lines around the table of elements were first used for a determinant by Cayley in 1841 (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 116). The notation shows all the elements in a clear arrangement, and so it caught on (CAJNOT2, PDF p. 116). From this comes the notation \(|A|\).

To calculate with the determinant of a square matrix we need rules of calculation for it. We will write the determinant of the matrix with the columns \(\vek u\), \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) briefly as \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w)\). By the definition, \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) = \vek u\cdot(\vek v\times\vek w)\).

Lemma 2.73 Properties of the determinant (lastnosti determinante)

For all vectors \(\vek u\), \(\vek u'\), \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\), all numbers \(k\) and every \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\):

  1. Cyclic exchange: \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) = \det(\vek v, \vek w, \vek u) = \det(\vek w, \vek u, \vek v)\).
  2. Linearity in each column: \(\det(\vek u + \vek u', \vek v, \vek w) = \det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) + \det(\vek u', \vek v, \vek w)\) and \(\det(k\,\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) = k\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w)\), and the same in the second and the third column.
  3. The determinant of a matrix with two equal columns is zero.
  4. If we exchange two columns, the determinant changes its sign, for example \(\det(\vek v, \vek u, \vek w) = -\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w)\).
  5. \(\det\mat I = 1\), the volume of the unit cube.
  6. When we exchange rows and columns, the determinant does not change: \(\det\mat A^\T = \det\mat A\).
Proof

We compute every item with components or reduce it to earlier items.

1. Cyclic exchange.

  1. By the formula for the vector product and (2.6),
    \[\vek u\cdot(\vek v\times\vek w) = u_{\mathrm{x}} (v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}} - v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}}) + u_{\mathrm{y}} (v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}} - v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}}) + u_{\mathrm{z}} (v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}} - v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}}) .\]
  2. We remove the brackets. We get six terms, \(u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(-u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  3. In the same way we compute \(\vek v\cdot(\vek w\times\vek u) = v_{\mathrm{x}} (w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{z}} - w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{y}}) + v_{\mathrm{y}} (w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{x}} - w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{z}}) + v_{\mathrm{z}} (w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{y}} - w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{x}})\) and get the terms \(v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(-v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(-v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  4. The order of factors in a product does not matter, so the terms match:
    \[\begin{aligned} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{z}} , & -v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= -u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{y}} , & v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}} u_{\mathrm{z}} &= u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{y}} , \\ -v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}} u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}} w_{\mathrm{z}} , & -v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -u_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}} w_{\mathrm{x}} , & v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}} u_{\mathrm{y}} &= u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}} w_{\mathrm{x}} . \end{aligned}\]
    The six terms agree with the same signs, hence \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) = \det(\vek v, \vek w, \vek u)\).
  5. We apply the equality of step 4 also to the triple \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\), \(\vek u\) and get \(\det(\vek v, \vek w, \vek u) = \det(\vek w, \vek u, \vek v)\).

2. Linearity.

  1. The vector \(\vek m = \vek v\times\vek w\) does not depend on the first column. By items 1 to 3 of the properties of the scalar product (lemma 2.12), \((\vek u + \vek u')\cdot\vek m = \vek u\cdot\vek m + \vek u'\cdot\vek m\) and \((k\,\vek u)\cdot\vek m = k\,(\vek u\cdot\vek m)\). This is linearity in the first column. Figure 2.213 shows what the sum means. We look at the body from the side, so that the plane of the edges \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) lies horizontally and the vector \(\vek m\) points up, perpendicular to it. With the unit normal \(\vek n = \vek m/|\vek m|\) we have \(\vek u\cdot\vek m = |\vek m|\,(\vek u\cdot\vek n)\), so the area \(|\vek m|\) of the base times the height \(h = \vek u\cdot\vek n\) of the tip of the vector \(\vek u\) above the plane, as in the proof of lemma 2.69, except that here the sign counts too. We lay the vector \(\vek u'\) on at the tip of the vector \(\vek u\). It moves the tip up by \(h' = \vek u'\cdot\vek n\), so the tip of the sum \(\vek u + \vek u'\) is \(h + h'\) above the plane. All three bodies have the same base, so their signed volumes add just as the heights do. On the right \(\vek u'\) points down, its height \(h'\) is negative, and the sum has the height \(h + h'\), smaller than \(h\). The signed volume then decreases, and the equation still holds.
  2. By item 1, \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) = \det(\vek v, \vek w, \vek u)\), where the second column \(\vek v\) has come to the first place. Linearity in the second column is therefore linearity in the first column of the determinant \(\det(\vek v, \vek w, \vek u)\), which holds by step 1.
  3. In the same way, by item 1, linearity in the third column follows from \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) = \det(\vek w, \vek u, \vek v)\).

3. Two equal columns.

  1. For every vector \(\vek v\), by the formula for the vector product, \(\vek v\times\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{z}} - v_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{y}},\ v_{\mathrm{z}} v_{\mathrm{x}} - v_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{z}},\ v_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} - v_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}}) = \vek 0\), since the parallelogram with the edges \(\vek v\) and \(\vek v\) is flat and has no area.
  2. If the second and the third column are equal, \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek v) = \vek u\cdot(\vek v\times\vek v) = \vek u\cdot\vek 0 = 0\).
  3. If the first and the second column are equal, then by item 1 \(\det(\vek u, \vek u, \vek w) = \det(\vek w, \vek u, \vek u)\), which is zero by step 2.
  4. If the first and the third column are equal, then by item 1 \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek u) = \det(\vek v, \vek u, \vek u)\), which is zero by step 2.

4. Exchanging two columns.

  1. Let us exchange the first and the second column. By item 3 the determinant with two equal columns \(\vek u + \vek v\) is zero: \(\det(\vek u + \vek v, \vek u + \vek v, \vek w) = 0\). Figure 2.214 shows the proof for the columns \(\vek u = (2, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek v = (1, 2, 0)\) in the plane of the \(x\) and \(y\) axes and for \(\vek w = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Such a matrix has zeros in the row \(z\) and the column \(z\), only the number \(1\) in the place \(zz\), so its determinant, as we computed above, is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} v_{\mathrm{y}} - u_{\mathrm{y}} v_{\mathrm{x}}\), the signed area of the parallelogram of the first two columns (figure 2.212). Both columns \(\vek u + \vek v = (3, 2, 0)\) lie on the same arrow, the parallelogram is flat and \(3 \cdot 2 - 2 \cdot 3 = 0\).
  2. By item 2 we split the left side first in the first and then in the second column:
    \[0 = \det(\vek u, \vek u, \vek w) + \det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) + \det(\vek v, \vek u, \vek w) + \det(\vek v, \vek v, \vek w) .\]
    In the figure these are the four parallelograms to the right of the equals sign.
  3. The first and the last term have two equal columns and are zero by item 3, their parallelograms are flat. There remains \(0 = \det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w) + \det(\vek v, \vek u, \vek w)\), so \(\det(\vek v, \vek u, \vek w) = -\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek w)\). In the figure \(\det(\vek u, \vek v, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = 2 \cdot 2 - 0 \cdot 1 = 4\) and \(\det(\vek v, \vek u, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) = 1 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot 2 = -4\). The parallelogram is the same, but the turn from the first column to the second goes the opposite way, and the sum of all four terms is \(0 + 4 - 4 + 0 = 0\).
  4. For the second and third or for the first and third column we repeat steps 1 to 3 with the sum \(\vek v + \vek w\) or \(\vek u + \vek w\) in the two places we exchange.

5. Identity matrix.

  1. The columns of the identity matrix are \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) (definition 1.108).
  2. By the formula for the vector product, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = (1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 1,\ 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 0) = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so \(\det\mat I = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\), the volume of the unit cube.

6. Transposed matrix.

  1. The transposed matrix has the entries \((\mat A^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}} = A_{\mathrm{ji}}\) (definition 1.101). We get \(\det\mat A^\T\) by exchanging the two indices of every entry in (2.70). In the table this means that the entry in the row \(x\) and the column \(y\) goes to the row \(y\) and the column \(x\), to the other side of the main diagonal, as a mirror image. Every term of the determinant \(\det\mat A^\T\) therefore has the same sign as the corresponding term in (2.70), but its coloured cells are mirrored.
  2. The term \(A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}}\) lies on the diagonal and does not change. The term \(A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}} A_{\mathrm{zx}}\) becomes \(A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{zy}} A_{\mathrm{xz}}\), which with the factors rearranged is the third term with a plus, \(A_{\mathrm{xz}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{zy}}\). The third term with a plus becomes \(A_{\mathrm{zx}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}}\), which is the second term with a plus. The mirroring exchanges the two.
  3. The terms with a minus: \(A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yz}} A_{\mathrm{zy}}\) becomes \(A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{zy}} A_{\mathrm{yz}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{zz}}\) becomes \(A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} A_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and \(A_{\mathrm{xz}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{zx}}\) becomes \(A_{\mathrm{zx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} A_{\mathrm{xz}}\). With the factors rearranged, each is the same term as before, since its coloured cells are symmetric about the diagonal.
  4. All six terms appear with the same signs in both determinants, so \(\det\mat A^\T = \det\mat A\).

Source: CM, properties (2), (4), (5), (6) (PDF p. 66), CM (2.2.21), (2.2.22) (PDF p. 45), KREYSZIG §7.7, Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 (PDF pp. 321-323). The proofs are not from the sources.

Every item has a geometric meaning (figure 2.216). Item 2 says that the volume doubles when we double one edge: when we lengthen the edge \(\vek u\) to \(2\vek u\), one more equal body stands on the body with the edges \(\vek u\), \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\). Item 3 says that a parallelepiped with two equal edges has no volume, since it is flattened into a plane: when we lay the edge \(\vek w\) onto the edge \(\vek v\), all that is left of the body is the parallelogram of the edges \(\vek u\) and \(\vek v\), which has no height. Item 4 says that exchanging two edges reverses the orientation but does not change the volume: the body is the same, but the turn from the first edge to the second goes from \(\vek u\) to \(\vek v\) for the order \(\vek u\), \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\), and from \(\vek v\) to \(\vek u\), the opposite way, for the order \(\vek v\), \(\vek u\), \(\vek w\). Item 1 is the exchange with which we proved the numerical form of the right-hand rule in lemma 2.71 on the direction of the vector product, written with the determinant: for vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) with \(\vek a\times\vek b \neq \vek 0\), \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek a\times\vek b) = \det(\vek a\times\vek b, \vek a, \vek b) = (\vek a\times\vek b)\cdot(\vek a\times\vek b) = |\vek a\times\vek b|^2 > 0\). And item 6 says that everything that holds for columns also holds for rows, since the rows of the matrix \(\mat A\) are the columns of the matrix \(\mat A^\T\). So it does not matter that CM and KREYSZIG write the scalar triple product as the determinant of the matrix whose rows are the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) (CM (2.3.9), PDF p. 66, KREYSZIG §9.3 (10), PDF p. 399): it is the determinant of the transposed matrix and therefore the same number.

Item 1 says that the same body can be placed on three bases and always gives the same volume (figure 2.217). On the left the base is the parallelogram of the edges \(\vek v\) and \(\vek w\) with the area \(|\vek v\times\vek w|\), the height of the body is the perpendicular component of the edge \(\vek u\), so the volume is \(|\vek u\cdot(\vek v\times\vek w)|\). In the middle the base is the parallelogram of the edges \(\vek w\) and \(\vek u\), the height is the perpendicular component of the edge \(\vek v\) and the volume is \(|\vek v\cdot(\vek w\times\vek u)|\). On the right the base is the parallelogram of the edges \(\vek u\) and \(\vek v\), the height is the perpendicular component of the edge \(\vek w\) and the volume is \(|\vek w\cdot(\vek u\times\vek v)|\). The body with the same edges is the same everywhere, so the three numbers have the same absolute value. That they also have the same sign, so that a cyclic shift keeps the orientation, is shown by the computation with components in the proof of item 1. The triple drawn is right-handed and all three numbers are positive, so the figure writes them without the absolute value. The dashed edges are the hidden ones.

Items 2 and 3 give one more rule, which we will need for the sheared cube. If we add a multiple of the second column to the first, the determinant does not change:

\[\det(\vek a + k\,\vek b, \vek b, \vek c) = \det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) + k\det(\vek b, \vek b, \vek c) = \det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) .\]

The first equality is linearity in the first column, the second is item 3. In figure 2.218 the left body is a box with the edge \(\vek a\) and the right one a parallelepiped with the edge \(\vek a + k\,\vek b\). The opposite face then moves by \(k\,\vek b\), parallel to the base. The base stays the same, and so does the height, because \((\vek a + k\,\vek b)\cdot\vek n = \vek a\cdot\vek n + k\,\vek b\cdot\vek n = \vek a\cdot\vek n\), since \(\vek b\) is perpendicular to the normal \(\vek n\) of the base. So the volume stays the same too. This is the reasoning of section 1.6.2, where the front face of the sheared cube became a parallelogram with the same base side and the same height, so its area did not change.

2.10.3 The determinant of a product

Two matrices can act one after the other. We got the matrix product in section 1.16 exactly from this: \((\mat A\mat B)\,\vek v = \mat A\,(\mat B\vek v)\) (item 1 of lemma 1.100, which follows from definition 1.99). We first send the vector with the matrix \(\mat B\), and then the result with the matrix \(\mat A\). How do volumes change on the way? Let us look in the plane, with the \(2 \times 2\) matrices

\[\mat B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat A\mat B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The matrix \(\mat B\) sends the unit square to the parallelogram of its columns \((2, 0)\) and \((1, 1)\), with the area \(\det\mat B = 2 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 0 = 2\). The matrix \(\mat A\) sends this parallelogram to the parallelogram of the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\), the vectors \((2, 2)\) and \((1, 3)\), with the area \(\det(\mat A\mat B) = 2 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 2 = 4\) (figure 2.219). The matrix \(\mat A\) alone sends the unit square to the parallelogram of its columns \((1, 1)\) and \((0, 2)\), with the area \(\det\mat A = 1 \cdot 2 - 0 \cdot 1 = 2\), so it multiplies the area by \(2\). It enlarged the parallelogram with the area \(2\) to the area \(4\) by the same factor two. So the areas multiply: \(4 = 2 \cdot 2\). Does a matrix multiply every area and every volume by the same factor, the absolute value of its determinant? If so, the determinant of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\) is the product of the determinants, at least in absolute value.

From history

The same question occupied two mathematicians independently in 1812. In the summer Cauchy, in Cherbourg, where he worked as an engineer, was looking for a generalisation of the formulas of Carl Friedrich Gauss, and found a theorem by which the determinant is multiplied by the determinant of the other matrix when one matrix is multiplied by another (MUIR, PDF p. 111, TIMO, PDF p. 116). When he returned to Paris, he visited Jacques Binet, who showed him a similar theorem. Binet had reached it by another route. The difference was only in the name: Binet called a resultant what Cauchy called a determinant (MUIR, PDF p. 111). On the same day, 30 November 1812, both read their memoirs at the Institute (MUIR, PDF p. 110). MUIR concludes that the theorem should bear both names. Binet obtained the more general theorem, of which Cauchy's is a special case, and Cauchy gave a satisfactory proof (MUIR, PDF p. 127).

The answer is yes for every parallelogram and every parallelepiped, and it holds even with the sign. The edges of a parallelepiped from one vertex are the columns of some matrix \(\mat B\), just as the edges of the parallelogram in figure 2.219 are the columns \((2, 0)\) and \((1, 1)\) of the matrix \(\mat B\). The matrix \(\mat A\) sends them to the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\), like the edges of the image \((2, 2)\) and \((1, 3)\). Binet and Cauchy showed that \(\det(\mat A\mat B) = \det\mat A\,\det\mat B\), so the area or volume \(\det\mat B\) is multiplied by \(\det\mat A\) and becomes \(\det(\mat A\mat B)\). For shapes of other kinds, a disc for example, we would have to fill the shape with ever smaller squares and take a limit, which we do not derive here.

Theorem 2.74 Determinant of a product (determinanta produkta)

For \(3 \times 3\) matrices \(\mat A\) and \(\mat B\),

\[\det(\mat A\mat B) = \det\mat A\,\det\mat B . \tag{2.72}\]
Proof

We write the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\) with the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\) and split the determinant by linearity. We call the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\) \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\).

  1. By (1.39) and definition 1.99 the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\) has the entries \((\mat A\mat B)_{\mathrm{ik}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}} B_{\mathrm{jk}} = A_{\mathrm{ix}} B_{\mathrm{xk}} + A_{\mathrm{iy}} B_{\mathrm{yk}} + A_{\mathrm{iz}} B_{\mathrm{zk}}\).
  2. The numbers \(A_{\mathrm{ix}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{iy}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{iz}}\) are the components \(i\) of the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\). So the column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\) is the vector \(B_{\mathrm{xk}}\,\vek a + B_{\mathrm{yk}}\,\vek b + B_{\mathrm{zk}}\,\vek c\).
  3. The determinant of the matrix \(\mat A\mat B\) is therefore
    \[\det(B_{\mathrm{xx}}\,\vek a + B_{\mathrm{yx}}\,\vek b + B_{\mathrm{zx}}\,\vek c,\ \ B_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\vek a + B_{\mathrm{yy}}\,\vek b + B_{\mathrm{zy}}\,\vek c,\ \ B_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\vek a + B_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\vek b + B_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\vek c) .\]
  1. By linearity in the first column (item 2 of lemma 2.73 on the properties of the determinant) we split it into three determinants, each of them by linearity in the second column into three, and each of these by linearity in the third column into three. We get \(3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 27\) terms, nine in each of the three grids. Each term chooses for each column one of the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\), for example the term \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{zz}}\det(\vek a, \vek a, \vek c)\).
  2. A term in which some vector repeats is zero by item 3 of the same lemma, like the example of step 4. Six terms remain, in which all three vectors appear, each once:
    \[\begin{aligned} \det(\mat A\mat B) = {}& B_{\mathrm{xx}} B_{\mathrm{yy}} B_{\mathrm{zz}} \det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) + B_{\mathrm{xx}} B_{\mathrm{zy}} B_{\mathrm{yz}} \det(\vek a, \vek c, \vek b) + B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{zz}} \det(\vek b, \vek a, \vek c) \\ &+ B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{zy}} B_{\mathrm{xz}} \det(\vek b, \vek c, \vek a) + B_{\mathrm{zx}} B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{yz}} \det(\vek c, \vek a, \vek b) + B_{\mathrm{zx}} B_{\mathrm{yy}} B_{\mathrm{xz}} \det(\vek c, \vek b, \vek a) . \end{aligned}\]
  3. We reduce each of the six determinants to \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) = \det\mat A\). By item 4 of the lemma, \(\det(\vek a, \vek c, \vek b)\), \(\det(\vek b, \vek a, \vek c)\) and \(\det(\vek c, \vek b, \vek a)\) equal \(-\det\mat A\), since each arises by one exchange of two columns. By item 1, \(\det(\vek b, \vek c, \vek a)\) and \(\det(\vek c, \vek a, \vek b)\) equal \(\det\mat A\).
  4. We take out \(\det\mat A\):
    \[\det(\mat A\mat B) = \det\mat A\,\big(B_{\mathrm{xx}} B_{\mathrm{yy}} B_{\mathrm{zz}} - B_{\mathrm{xx}} B_{\mathrm{zy}} B_{\mathrm{yz}} - B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{zz}} + B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{zy}} B_{\mathrm{xz}} + B_{\mathrm{zx}} B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{yz}} - B_{\mathrm{zx}} B_{\mathrm{yy}} B_{\mathrm{xz}}\big) .\]
  5. We compare the bracket with (2.70) for the matrix \(\mat B\). The term \(B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{zy}} B_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is, with the factors rearranged, \(B_{\mathrm{xz}} B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{zy}}\), the term \(B_{\mathrm{zx}} B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{yz}}\) is \(B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{yz}} B_{\mathrm{zx}}\), \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} B_{\mathrm{zy}} B_{\mathrm{yz}}\) is \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} B_{\mathrm{yz}} B_{\mathrm{zy}}\), \(B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is \(B_{\mathrm{xy}} B_{\mathrm{yx}} B_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and \(B_{\mathrm{zx}} B_{\mathrm{yy}} B_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is \(B_{\mathrm{xz}} B_{\mathrm{yy}} B_{\mathrm{zx}}\). The signs agree, so the bracket is \(\det\mat B\).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.8, Theorem 4 (10) (PDF p. 333), for \(n \times n\) matrices, CM, property (1) (PDF p. 66). The proof is not from the sources.

The proof showed where the rule comes from. The columns of the product are combinations of the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\) with numbers from the matrix \(\mat B\). In figure 2.220 the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\) are the vectors \(\vek a = (1, 1)\) and \(\vek b = (0, 2)\). The first column of the product is \((2, 2) = 2 \cdot (1, 1) + 0 \cdot (0, 2)\), the vector \(\vek a\) laid down twice. The second is \((1, 3) = 1 \cdot (1, 1) + 1 \cdot (0, 2)\), the vector \(\vek b\) with the vector \(\vek a\) placed at its tip. The numbers in front of \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) are the columns \((2, 0)\) and \((1, 1)\) of the matrix \(\mat B\). Linearity splits the determinant of the product into terms, equal columns drop out, and exchanges of columns give exactly the signs with which the determinant of \(\mat B\) is built from its numbers.

For \(2 \times 2\) matrices the theorem holds as well. We put both into a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with \(1\) at the place \(zz\) and zeros elsewhere in the row and the column \(z\), as in section 2.10.2, and call the larger matrices \(\mat A'\) and \(\mat B'\) (figure 2.222). In their product the entry \(zz\) is \(0 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1\), the other entries of the row and the column \(z\) are zero, because each of their terms has a factor zero, and the remaining four entries are the entries of the product of the \(2 \times 2\) matrices. So the product of the larger matrices is the larger matrix of the product. The determinant of a larger matrix equals, by (2.70), the determinant of the smaller one, as we saw in section 2.10.2: the parallelepiped of its columns has as its base the parallelogram of the columns of the smaller matrix and the height \(1\). By theorem 2.74 for \(3 \times 3\) matrices, therefore,

\[\det(\mat A\mat B) = \det(\mat A'\mat B') = \det\mat A'\,\det\mat B' = \det\mat A\,\det\mat B .\]

This agrees with the determinants \(2\), \(2\) and \(4\) of the larger matrices and with figure 2.219, where \(\det(\mat A\mat B) = 4\) \(= 2 \cdot 2\).

The first use concerns turned axes. In section 2.9 we wrote the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) so that its rows are the unit vectors of the turned axes \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}}\) (definition 2.44), and we saw that it is orthogonal, \(\mat Q\mat Q^\T = \mat I\) (lemma 2.47 on the orthogonality of the rotation matrix). By theorem 2.74 on the determinant of a product and items 5 and 6 of the lemma on the properties of the determinant,

\[\det\mat Q\,\det\mat Q^\T = \det\mat I = 1 , \qquad \det\mat Q^\T = \det\mat Q , \qquad \text{so} \qquad (\det\mat Q)^2 = 1 .\]

The determinant of an orthogonal matrix is therefore \(1\) or \(-1\). The columns of the matrix \(\mat Q^\T\) are the rows of the matrix \(\mat Q\), so \(\det\mat Q = \det\mat Q^\T = \bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\cdot(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\times\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}})\). Since the determinant is \(1\) or \(-1\), this scalar triple product is \(1\) when the turned axes are again right-handed in the sense of definition 2.70, and \(-1\) when they are the mirror image of right-handed ones. The absolute value is \(1\) in both cases, because the unit vectors of the turned axes are perpendicular to each other and have the length \(1\), so they span a cube with the edge \(1\). In the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) this is a square with the area \(1\), equal to the unit square of the vectors \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) (figure 2.223). Take the axes turned about the axis \(z\) with the pair \(c = 0{,}6\), \(s = 0{,}8\), for which \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), so that \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (c, s, 0)\), \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (-s, c, 0)\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Then

\[\mat Q = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & 0{,}8 & 0 \\ -0{,}8 & 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

and by (2.70) \(\det\mat Q = 0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}6 \cdot 1 - 0{,}8 \cdot (-0{,}8) \cdot 1 = 0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\), since the other four terms are zero. This turn of the axes has \(\det\mat Q = 1\), so it changes neither volumes nor orientation: the turned square has the area \(1\) like the unit square, and the arc from \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) to \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) runs the same way as the arc from \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). A mirrored system of axes would have \(\det\mat Q = -1\). For \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}} = (0{,}6,\ 0{,}8,\ 0)\) and \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}} = (0{,}8,\ -0{,}6,\ 0)\), by (2.70) \(\det\mat Q = 0{,}6 \cdot (-0{,}6) \cdot 1 - 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}8 \cdot 1 = -0{,}36 - 0{,}64 = -1\). The square still has the area \(1\), but the arc from \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{x}}\) to \(\bar{\vek e}_{\mathrm{y}}\) runs the opposite way to the arc from \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\).

2.10.4 Zero determinant and the inverse matrix

Let us return to the question from the beginning of the section: when does a matrix \(\mat A\) send some nonzero vector \(\vek v\) to the zero vector? The product of a matrix and a vector can be read in two ways. The component \(i\) of the vector \(\mat A\vek v\) is

\[(\mat A\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}} = A_{\mathrm{ix}} v_{\mathrm{x}} + A_{\mathrm{iy}} v_{\mathrm{y}} + A_{\mathrm{iz}} v_{\mathrm{z}} .\]

The numbers \(A_{\mathrm{ix}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{iy}}\) and \(A_{\mathrm{iz}}\) are the components \(i\) of the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\), so \(\mat A\vek v = v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek a + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek b + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek c\), the sum of the columns multiplied by the components of the vector \(\vek v\). But the same numbers \(A_{\mathrm{ix}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{iy}}\), \(A_{\mathrm{iz}}\) are also the components of the row \(i\) written as a vector, and by (2.6) \((\mat A\vek v)_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the scalar product of the row \(i\) with the vector \(\vek v\). So the equality \(\mat A\vek v = \vek 0\) means that \(\vek v\) is perpendicular to all three rows.

The first way gives us the idea for one direction. If \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek a + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek b + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek c = \vek 0\) and, for example, \(v_{\mathrm{x}} \neq 0\), the column \(\vek a\) is a combination of the other two, and the parallelepiped of the columns is flattened. The second way gives us the idea for the other direction. We call the rows of the matrix \(\mat A\), written as vectors, \(\vek p\), \(\vek q\) and \(\vek r\). If the determinant is zero, then by item 6 of lemma 2.73 on the properties of the determinant the rows too are the edges of a flattened parallelepiped, so they lie in one plane. A vector perpendicular to this plane is perpendicular to all three rows (figure 2.227 shows such a case). Such a vector is given by the vector product of two rows.

Lemma 2.75 Zero determinant (ničelna determinanta)

For a \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\), \(\det\mat A = 0\) exactly when there is a vector \(\vek v \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat A\vek v = \vek 0\).

Proof

We must prove two directions. We call the columns of the matrix \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\), and its rows, written as vectors, \(\vek p = (A_{\mathrm{xx}}, A_{\mathrm{xy}}, A_{\mathrm{xz}})\), \(\vek q = (A_{\mathrm{yx}}, A_{\mathrm{yy}}, A_{\mathrm{yz}})\) and \(\vek r = (A_{\mathrm{zx}}, A_{\mathrm{zy}}, A_{\mathrm{zz}})\).

1. From \(\mat A\vek v = \vek 0\) with \(\vek v \neq \vek 0\) follows \(\det\mat A = 0\).

  1. As we computed before the lemma, \(\mat A\vek v = v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek a + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek b + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek c\), so the sum of the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\), multiplied by \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\), is \(\vek 0\): \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\,\vek a + v_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek b + v_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek c = \vek 0\).
  2. The vector \(\vek v\) is not the zero vector, so at least one of its components is not zero. Let it be \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\). We divide the equality of step 1 by \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\) and express \(\vek a = -(v_{\mathrm{y}}/v_{\mathrm{x}})\,\vek b - (v_{\mathrm{z}}/v_{\mathrm{x}})\,\vek c\).
  3. By linearity in the first column (item 2 of lemma 2.73 on the properties of the determinant) the determinant splits into two terms, one for each part of the column \(\vek a\):
    \[\det\mat A = \det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) = -\frac{v_{\mathrm{y}}}{v_{\mathrm{x}}}\det(\vek b, \vek b, \vek c) - \frac{v_{\mathrm{z}}}{v_{\mathrm{x}}}\det(\vek c, \vek b, \vek c) .\]
  4. Both determinants on the right have two equal columns and are zero by item 3 of the same lemma. The parallelepiped is flat, since all three edges lie in one plane. So \(\det\mat A = 0\).
  5. If \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\) but \(v_{\mathrm{y}}\) or \(v_{\mathrm{z}}\) is not zero, we proceed in the same way. We express the column \(\vek b\) or \(\vek c\), split it by linearity in the second or the third column, and in each term one column repeats.

2. From \(\det\mat A = 0\) follows that there is \(\vek v \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat A\vek v = \vek 0\).

  1. The matrix with the columns \(\vek p\), \(\vek q\), \(\vek r\) is \(\mat A^\T\) (definition 1.101). By item 6 of the lemma, \(\det(\vek p, \vek q, \vek r) = \det\mat A^\T = \det\mat A = 0\). By the definition this is \(\vek p\cdot(\vek q\times\vek r) = 0\), the rows lie in one plane, and by item 1 of the same lemma also \(\det(\vek r, \vek p, \vek q) = \vek r\cdot(\vek p\times\vek q)\) and \(\det(\vek q, \vek r, \vek p) = \vek q\cdot(\vek r\times\vek p)\) are zero.
  2. Let \(\vek p\times\vek q \neq \vek 0\). We take \(\vek v = \vek p\times\vek q\), perpendicular to the plane of the rows like the blue vector in figure 2.227. By item 3 of the lemma, \(\vek p\cdot\vek v = \det(\vek p, \vek p, \vek q) = 0\) and \(\vek q\cdot\vek v = \det(\vek q, \vek p, \vek q) = 0\), and by step 1, \(\vek r\cdot\vek v = 0\). All three components of the vector \(\mat A\vek v\) are zero, and \(\vek v \neq \vek 0\).
  3. If \(\vek p\times\vek q = \vek 0\) but \(\vek q\times\vek r\) or \(\vek r\times\vek p\) is not zero, we proceed as in step 2 with \(\vek v = \vek q\times\vek r\) or \(\vek v = \vek r\times\vek p\). The scalar product with the third row is zero by step 1.
  1. There remains the case in which all three vector products of rows are zero. If all rows are zero, then \(\mat A\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek 0\), and we take \(\vek v = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). Otherwise at least one row is nonzero. We call it \(\vek m\).
  2. Let us show that every row \(\vek w\) is a multiple of the row \(\vek m\). We have \(\vek m\times\vek w = \vek 0\), because this is one of the products of step 4 or its negative, or else \(\vek w = \vek m\) and \(\vek m\times\vek m = \vek 0\) (item 1 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product). Let \(\vek e = \vek m/|\vek m|\). By item 5 of lemma 2.34 on the properties of the vector product, \(|\vek m\times\vek w|^2 = |\vek m|^2|\vek w|^2 - (\vek m\cdot\vek w)^2\), so by item 3 of lemma 2.14 on splitting a vector
    \[|\vek w - (\vek w\cdot\vek e)\,\vek e|^2 = |\vek w|^2 - \frac{(\vek m\cdot\vek w)^2}{|\vek m|^2} = \frac{|\vek m\times\vek w|^2}{|\vek m|^2} = 0 .\]
    A vector of length zero is the zero vector, so \(\vek w = (\vek w\cdot\vek e)\,\vek e\), a multiple of the row \(\vek m\).
  1. We look for a nonzero vector \(\vek v\) perpendicular to \(\vek m = (m_{\mathrm{x}}, m_{\mathrm{y}}, m_{\mathrm{z}})\). If \(m_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(m_{\mathrm{y}}\) are not both zero, we take \(\vek v = (-m_{\mathrm{y}}, m_{\mathrm{x}}, 0)\), which lies in the \(x\), \(y\) plane, is not the zero vector and for which \(\vek m\cdot\vek v = -m_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{y}} + m_{\mathrm{y}} m_{\mathrm{x}} + 0 = 0\). Otherwise \(\vek m = (0, 0, m_{\mathrm{z}})\), and we take \(\vek v = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  2. By step 5 every row equals \(k\,\vek m\) for some number \(k\), and \((k\,\vek m)\cdot\vek v = k\,(\vek m\cdot\vek v) = 0\). So \(\mat A\vek v = \vek 0\).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.7, Theorem 4(b) (PDF p. 324), for \(n \times n\) matrices. CM, property (6) (PDF pp. 66-67), treats only the direction from a column that is a multiple of another column to a zero determinant. The proof is not from the sources.

The lemma says that the determinant detects whether a matrix loses some nonzero vector. Let us test it on the pure shear from the beginning of the section. The cube is pulled by four forces along its faces, of size \(\tau_0\) per unit area (figure 2.77, left), and the stress matrix has the rows \((0, 0, \tau_0)\), \((0, 0, 0)\) and \((\tau_0, 0, 0)\). The matrix \(\ten\sigma - \tau_0\,\mat I\) has the rows

\[\vek p = (-\tau_0, 0, \tau_0) , \qquad \vek q = (0, -\tau_0, 0) , \qquad \vek r = (\tau_0, 0, -\tau_0) .\]

By (2.70) its determinant is \((-\tau_0)(-\tau_0)(-\tau_0) + 0 + 0 - 0 - 0 - \tau_0 \cdot (-\tau_0) \cdot \tau_0 = -\tau_0^3 + \tau_0^3 = 0\), since of the six terms only the first and the last have no zero factor. By the lemma there is therefore a nonzero vector that the matrix sends to zero. The proof also finds it. The vector product of the first two rows is

\[\vek p\times\vek q = \big(0 \cdot 0 - \tau_0 \cdot (-\tau_0),\ \tau_0 \cdot 0 - (-\tau_0) \cdot 0,\ (-\tau_0)(-\tau_0) - 0 \cdot 0\big) = \tau_0^2\,(1, 0, 1) .\]

This is the direction of the normal of the face perpendicular to the diagonal \(AC\), which we found in section 2.6.6 (the blue normal \(\vek n\) on the diagonal face \(BD\), figure 2.77, right). All three rows lie in the plane perpendicular to the vector \((1, 0, 1)\), since \(\vek r = -\vek p\) and \(\vek p\cdot(1, 0, 1) = 0\), \(\vek q\cdot(1, 0, 1) = 0\) (figure 2.227). For the matrix \(\mat A\) of figure 2.210, with the determinant \(12\), the lemma says the opposite: \(\mat A\vek v = \vek 0\) holds only for \(\vek v = \vek 0\).

Now we can also answer the question from section 1.16 of when a matrix has an inverse matrix, that is, a matrix \(\mat B\) with \(\mat B\mat A = \mat A\mat B = \mat I\) (definition 1.110). The scalar triple product gives us the idea. We draw it on the parallelepiped of the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\) of figure 2.210, with the columns \(\vek a = (1, 1, 2)\), \(\vek b = (2, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek c = (1, 3, 0)\), three times. In the left panel the columns \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) span the base. The vector \(\vek b\times\vek c\) is perpendicular to both, so it points along the normal of this face, like the vector \(\vek n\) in figure 2.202. Its scalar product with the third column \(\vek a\) is \(\det\mat A\), the length \(|\vek b\times\vek c| = 6\), the area of the base, times the height \(h = 2\), that is \(12\). If we divide the vector \(\vek b\times\vek c\) by \(\det\mat A\), its scalar products with the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) are \(1\), \(0\), \(0\), exactly like those of the first row of the identity matrix with the columns of the identity matrix. We do the same with the vectors \(\vek c\times\vek a\) and \(\vek a\times\vek b\). The first is perpendicular to the face of the columns \(\vek c\) and \(\vek a\) in the middle panel, the second to the face of the columns \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) on the right. There too the area of the base times the height of the third column is the volume of the same body, \(12\).

Theorem 2.76 Inverse via the determinant (inverzna matrika z determinanto)

A \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\) has an inverse matrix exactly when \(\det\mat A \neq 0\). Then the inverse matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\) is the matrix with the rows

\[\frac{\vek b\times\vek c}{\det\mat A} , \qquad \frac{\vek c\times\vek a}{\det\mat A} , \qquad \frac{\vek a\times\vek b}{\det\mat A} , \tag{2.73}\]

where \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) are the columns of the matrix \(\mat A\).

Proof

First we show that a matrix with a zero determinant has no inverse matrix. Then we show that for \(\det\mat A \neq 0\) the matrix with the rows (2.73) is the inverse matrix.

  1. Suppose that \(\mat A\) has an inverse matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\). By theorem 2.74 on the determinant of a product and item 5 of lemma 2.73 on the properties of the determinant, \(\det\mat A\,\det\mat A^{-1} = \det(\mat A\mat A^{-1}) = \det\mat I = 1\). So \(\det\mat A\) is not zero. In figure 2.229 this computation is a way there and back. At the top the matrix \(\mat A\) sends the unit cube with the volume \(1\) to the parallelepiped with the volume \(\det\mat A = 12\). The matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\) brings it back to the cube, so it must multiply the volume \(12\) by \(1/12\). At the bottom the matrix \(\ten\sigma - \tau_0\,\mat I\) of pure shear with \(\tau_0 = 1\), which, as we computed for the lemma, has the determinant \(0\), flattens the cube into a rectangle with the volume \(0\). It lies in the plane of the columns, which, since the matrix is symmetric, equal the rows \(\vek p\), \(\vek q\), \(\vek r\) of figure 2.227. A matrix \(\mat B\) that brought the rectangle back to the cube would have to turn the volume \(0\) into \(1\). No matrix can do this, since \(\det\mat B \cdot 0 = 0\).
  2. Let \(\det\mat A \neq 0\) and let \(\mat B\) be the matrix with the rows (2.73). By definition 1.99 the entry \(ij\) of the matrix \(\mat B\mat A\) is the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} B_{\mathrm{ik}} A_{\mathrm{kj}}\), that is, the scalar product of the row \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat B\) with the column \(j\) of the matrix \(\mat A\).
  3. Row \(x\): the scalar product of the vector \(\vek b\times\vek c\) with the column \(\vek a\) is \(\det\mat A\) (item 1 of lemma 2.12 and definition 2.72), and with the columns \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) it is \(\det(\vek b, \vek b, \vek c) = 0\) and \(\det(\vek c, \vek b, \vek c) = 0\) (item 3 of the lemma on the properties of the determinant). After dividing by \(\det\mat A\), the entries of the row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat B\mat A\) are \(1\), \(0\), \(0\).
  4. Row \(y\): the scalar product of the vector \(\vek c\times\vek a\) with the column \(\vek b\) is \(\det(\vek b, \vek c, \vek a) = \det\mat A\) (item 1 of the lemma on the properties of the scalar product and item 1 of the lemma on the properties of the determinant), and with the columns \(\vek a\) and \(\vek c\) it is \(\det(\vek a, \vek c, \vek a) = 0\) and \(\det(\vek c, \vek c, \vek a) = 0\) (item 3 of the lemma on the properties of the determinant). The entries of the row \(y\) are \(0\), \(1\), \(0\).
  5. Row \(z\): the scalar product of the vector \(\vek a\times\vek b\) with the column \(\vek c\) is \(\det(\vek c, \vek a, \vek b) = \det\mat A\), and with the columns \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) it is \(\det(\vek a, \vek a, \vek b) = 0\) and \(\det(\vek b, \vek a, \vek b) = 0\), for the same reasons as in step 4. The entries of the row \(z\) are \(0\), \(0\), \(1\).
  6. By steps 3 to 5, \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\).
  7. We still have to show \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\). By the theorem on the determinant of a product, \(\det\mat B\,\det\mat A = \det(\mat B\mat A) = 1\), so \(\det\mat B \neq 0\). We repeat steps 2 to 6 for the matrix \(\mat B\) and get a matrix \(\mat C\) with \(\mat C\mat B = \mat I\).
  8. In a product of three matrices we may group the factors as we like (item 2 of lemma 1.100 on the properties of the matrix product), so \(\mat C = \mat C\mat I = \mat C\,(\mat B\mat A) = (\mat C\mat B)\,\mat A = \mat I\mat A = \mat A\). From \(\mat C\mat B = \mat I\) therefore follows \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\).
  9. The matrix \(\mat B\) fulfils both conditions of definition 1.110, so it is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.8, Theorem 1 (PDF p. 327) and Theorem 2 (4) (PDF p. 330), for \(n \times n\) matrices, CM (2.3.11) (PDF p. 67). The sources write the inverse matrix with cofactors. The proof is not from the sources.

Let us test it on the matrix \(\mat A\) of figure 2.210, with the columns \(\vek a = (1, 1, 2)\), \(\vek b = (2, 0, 0)\), \(\vek c = (1, 3, 0)\) and the determinant \(12\). We compute the vector products by the formula for the vector product: \(\vek b\times\vek c = (0, 0, 6)\), as above, \(\vek c\times\vek a = (3 \cdot 2 - 0 \cdot 1,\ 0 \cdot 1 - 1 \cdot 2,\ 1 \cdot 1 - 3 \cdot 1) =\) \((6, -2, -2)\) and \(\vek a\times\vek b = (1 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot 0,\ 2 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 0,\ 1 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 2) =\) \((0, 4, -2)\). Therefore

\[\mat A^{-1} = \frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 6 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Let us check two entries of the product \(\mat A^{-1}\mat A\).
