The row \(y\) times the column \(x\) is \((6 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 1 - 2 \cdot 2)/12 = 0\), and the row \(y\) times the column \(y\) is \((6 \cdot 2 - 2 \cdot 0 - 2 \cdot 0)/12 = 1\), as the identity matrix requires. The other seven entries also agree with the identity matrix, and so do all nine entries of the product \(\mat A\mat A^{-1}\).

The theorem and the lemma together say this. For a \(3 \times 3\) matrix three claims are equivalent: the determinant is not zero, the matrix sends no nonzero vector to the zero vector, and the matrix has an inverse matrix. For the matrix of pure shear in the bottom row of figure 2.229 none of the three claims holds. The volume of the image of the cube is \(0\), the vector \(\vek v = (1, 0, 1)\), the diagonal of the front face of the cube, goes to the zero vector, so the corners \(O\) and \(V\) go to the same point \(O\), and there is no way back, since no matrix can bring the point \(O\) back to both \(O\) and \(V\). This keeps the promise of section 1.16.5: the second claim gives the first by lemma 2.75 on a zero determinant, and the first gives the third by theorem 2.76. In section 1.16 we said that books call a matrix without an inverse matrix singular (singularna). By the theorem this is exactly a matrix with determinant zero, so CM uses the word in both senses (CM, PDF pp. 65, 67). The inverse matrix has the determinant \(1/\det\mat A\), for the matrix \(\mat A\) of the figure \(1/12\), which follows from step 1 of the proof. CM writes the matrix (2.73) as \(\adj\mat A/\det\mat A\) (CM (2.3.11), PDF p. 67). The matrix \(\adj\mat A\), which CM calls the adjunct, has exactly the vectors \(\vek b\times\vek c\), \(\vek c\times\vek a\) and \(\vek a\times\vek b\) as its rows.

2.10.5 Change of volume

Let us return to the body. Let the displacement field of the body be continuously differentiable (definition 1.91), let \(P\) be a point inside the body, \(\mat H\) the displacement gradient at \(P\), the matrix with the entries \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\,(P)\) (definition 1.112), and \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) the deformation gradient at \(P\) (definition 1.113). From \(P\) we draw three short fibres with the vectors \(h\,\vek a\), \(h\,\vek b\) and \(h\,\vek c\), where \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) are chosen vectors that form a right-handed triple, and \(h > 0\) is a small number. The fibres span a small parallelepiped, a piece of the body at \(P\) (figure 2.230, left). By lemma 2.69 on the volume of a parallelepiped and linearity of the determinant in each column, it has the volume

\[\det(h\,\vek a, h\,\vek b, h\,\vek c) = h^3\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) ,\]

which is positive because the triple is right-handed.

Where do the fibres go? Let \(A = P + h\,\vek a\) be the end point of the first fibre. By (1.16) the vector of the fibre after loading is \(\overrightarrow{P_1 A_1} = h\,\vek a + \big(\vek u(A) - \vek u(P)\big)\). We write the difference of displacements by theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step, for each component separately, with the step \(h\,\vek a\):

\[u_{\mathrm{i}}(A) - u_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,h\,a_{\mathrm{j}} + R_{\mathrm{i}} ,\]

where \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the remainder of the component \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\). The sum is the component \(i\) of the vector \(\mat H(h\,\vek a)\) ((1.39)). The component \(i\) of the vector \(h\,\vek a\) is \(h\,a_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} I_{\mathrm{ij}}\,h\,a_{\mathrm{j}}\), because the row \(i\) of the identity matrix has a single nonzero entry, \(1\) in the column \(i\). We add the two sums:

\[\overrightarrow{P_1 A_1} = (\mat I + \mat H)(h\,\vek a) + (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}}) = \mat F(h\,\vek a) + (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}}) .\]

The remainders are small compared with the length of the fibre. By theorem 1.89, for every \(\eta > 0\) and small enough \(h\) each of them is at most \(\eta\,h\,|\vek a|\) in absolute value. The same holds for the other two fibres. If we leave the remainders out, the vectors of the fibres after loading are \(\mat F(h\,\vek a)\), \(\mat F(h\,\vek b)\) and \(\mat F(h\,\vek c)\), and the piece after loading is the parallelepiped they span (figure 2.230, right). This is a simplification. The real piece differs from this parallelepiped by the remainders: its edges curve slightly, and the end points of the fibres are not exactly at the tips of the vectors \(\mat F(h\,\vek a)\), \(\mat F(h\,\vek b)\), \(\mat F(h\,\vek c)\). How large the error is we will check on the hanging bar below. The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \(\mat F\) times the edge vectors is given by the first item of the next lemma. The second item tells what the determinant of the matrix \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) becomes when all entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) are small, which we will need for the relation with strains.

Lemma 2.77 Change of volume (sprememba prostornine)

Let \(\mat F\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix and \(\mat H = \mat F - \mat I\). Then:

  1. For all vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\),
    \[\det(\mat F\vek a, \mat F\vek b, \mat F\vek c) = \det\mat F\,\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) . \tag{2.74}\]
    So the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors \(\mat F\vek a\), \(\mat F\vek b\) and \(\mat F\vek c\) has \(|\det\mat F|\) times the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\). When \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) \neq 0\), that is, when the parallelepiped of the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\) is not flat, the two triples have the same orientation exactly when \(\det\mat F > 0\).
  2. If all entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) are at most \(g\) in absolute value, then \(\det\mat F\) differs from \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3\).

When \(\mat F\) is the deformation gradient at a point of a body, the number \(J = \det\mat F\) is called the Jacobian (Jacobijeva determinanta).

Proof

In item 1 we write the matrix with the columns \(\mat F\vek a\), \(\mat F\vek b\), \(\mat F\vek c\) as a product of two matrices, in item 2 we write out the determinant of the matrix \(\mat I + \mat H\) by (2.70).

1. Volume of the parallelepiped.

  1. Let \(\mat M\) be the matrix with the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\). By definition 1.99 the entry \(ik\) of the matrix \(\mat F\mat M\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} F_{\mathrm{ij}} M_{\mathrm{jk}}\). The numbers \(M_{\mathrm{jk}}\) with \(k\) fixed and \(j = x, y, z\) are the components of the column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat M\), so by (1.39) the column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat F\mat M\) is \(\mat F\) times the column \(k\) of the matrix \(\mat M\).
  2. So the columns of the matrix \(\mat F\mat M\) are \(\mat F\vek a\), \(\mat F\vek b\) and \(\mat F\vek c\), and \(\det(\mat F\vek a, \mat F\vek b, \mat F\vek c) = \det(\mat F\mat M)\).
  3. By theorem 2.74 on the determinant of a product, \(\det(\mat F\mat M) = \det\mat F\,\det\mat M = \det\mat F\,\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)\). This is (2.74).
  4. By lemma 2.69 on the volume of a parallelepiped, the volumes of the two parallelepipeds are the absolute values of the two sides of (2.74). The absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values, so the first volume is \(|\det\mat F|\) times the second.
  5. Let \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) \neq 0\). By definition 2.70 the orientation of a triple is the sign of its scalar triple product, that is, of the determinant of its vectors. By (2.74) the scalar triple product of the triple \(\mat F\vek a\), \(\mat F\vek b\), \(\mat F\vek c\) is the number \(\det\mat F\) times the nonzero number \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)\). For \(\det\mat F > 0\) it therefore has the same sign as \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)\), for \(\det\mat F < 0\) the opposite sign, and for \(\det\mat F = 0\) it is zero, and the triple \(\mat F\vek a\), \(\mat F\vek b\), \(\mat F\vek c\) has no orientation. So the two triples have the same orientation exactly when \(\det\mat F > 0\).

2. Small entries of the matrix \(\mat H\).

  1. The entries of the matrix \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) are \(F_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{yy}} = 1 + H_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(F_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1 + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) on the diagonal and \(F_{\mathrm{ij}} = H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) off it.
  2. The first term of (2.70) is the product of the diagonal entries. When we multiply out the brackets, we get
    \[(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}})(1 + H_{\mathrm{yy}})(1 + H_{\mathrm{zz}}) = 1 + (H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}) + (H_{\mathrm{xx}} H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{xx}} H_{\mathrm{zz}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} H_{\mathrm{zz}}) + H_{\mathrm{xx}} H_{\mathrm{yy}} H_{\mathrm{zz}} .\]
    For positive entries the left side is the volume of a box with edges \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(1 + H_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(1 + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) (figure 2.231). The planes that cut the length \(1\) off each edge cut the box into eight pieces. The unit cube is the term \(1\). The three slabs, of thickness \(H_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(H_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{zz}}\), are the first bracket. The three bars, whose cross-section is a rectangle with two of these thicknesses, are the second bracket, and the tiny cube in the corner is the last term. So multiplying out the brackets means adding up the volumes of the pieces.
  3. The second and the third term of (2.70), \(H_{\mathrm{xy}} H_{\mathrm{yz}} H_{\mathrm{zx}}\) and \(H_{\mathrm{xz}} H_{\mathrm{yx}} H_{\mathrm{zy}}\), have no diagonal entries and are products of three entries of the matrix \(\mat H\).
  4. The terms with a minus have one diagonal entry each. For example \(-F_{\mathrm{xx}} F_{\mathrm{yz}} F_{\mathrm{zy}} = -(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}})\,H_{\mathrm{yz}} H_{\mathrm{zy}} = -H_{\mathrm{yz}} H_{\mathrm{zy}} - H_{\mathrm{xx}} H_{\mathrm{yz}} H_{\mathrm{zy}}\). Likewise \(-F_{\mathrm{xy}} F_{\mathrm{yx}} F_{\mathrm{zz}} = -H_{\mathrm{xy}} H_{\mathrm{yx}} - H_{\mathrm{xy}} H_{\mathrm{yx}} H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) and \(-F_{\mathrm{xz}} F_{\mathrm{yy}} F_{\mathrm{zx}} = -H_{\mathrm{xz}} H_{\mathrm{zx}} - H_{\mathrm{xz}} H_{\mathrm{yy}} H_{\mathrm{zx}}\).
  5. We order the terms by how many entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) they contain. The products of three entries from steps 2, 3 and 4 are exactly the six terms of (2.70) for the matrix \(\mat H\), so
    \[\begin{aligned} \det\mat F = 1 &+ (H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}) \\ &+ \big(H_{\mathrm{xx}} H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{xx}} H_{\mathrm{zz}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} H_{\mathrm{zz}} \\ &\qquad - H_{\mathrm{xy}} H_{\mathrm{yx}} - H_{\mathrm{xz}} H_{\mathrm{zx}} - H_{\mathrm{yz}} H_{\mathrm{zy}}\big) \\ &+ \det\mat H . \end{aligned} \tag{2.75}\]
  6. The second bracket has six products of two entries of the matrix \(\mat H\), each at most \(g \cdot g = g^2\) in absolute value, just as the cross-section of a bar is at most \(g^2\), so the bracket is at most \(6g^2\).
  7. The determinant of \(\mat H\) has six products of three entries, each at most \(g^3\) in absolute value, like the volume of the cube in the corner, so \(|\det\mat H| \le 6g^3\).
  8. By steps 5 to 7, \(\big|\det\mat F - (1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}})\big| \le 6g^2 + 6g^3\).

Source: CM (3.3.18)-(3.3.20) (PDF pp. 125-126), BOWER §2.1.4 (PDF pp. 46-47) and §2.1.9 (PDF p. 51). The name: CM (PDF p. 119), BOWER (PDF p. 46). The error bound and the proofs are not from the sources.

For our three fibres the ratio between the volume of the parallelepiped after loading and the volume of the piece before loading is therefore

\[\frac{\det\big(\mat F(h\,\vek a), \mat F(h\,\vek b), \mat F(h\,\vek c)\big)}{\det(h\,\vek a, h\,\vek b, h\,\vek c)} = \frac{\det\mat F\ h^3\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)}{h^3\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)} = J ,\]

if \(J > 0\). The ratio depends neither on the length of the fibres nor on their directions. The Jacobian is a property of the displacement field at the point \(P\), not of the chosen piece. CM therefore describes it as the local ratio between the volume after loading and the volume before loading (CM, PDF p. 126). It is named after the German mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi (1804-1851), who also contributed to mechanics (KREYSZIG §10.3, PDF p. 456, footnote 3).

How good is the simplification of leaving out the remainders? Let us check on the hanging bar. A steel bar of length 10 m hangs under its own weight, held only at the centre \(O\) of its upper end, with the top face pulled up evenly, as in section 1.7.1. The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down, and \(P = (5\ \text{m},\ 4\ \text{mm},\ 0)\). From the table of partial derivatives at the point \(P\) in section 1.7.2,

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} & -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} ,\]

and by (2.70) \(J - 1 = 7{,}80798 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Now let us take three fibres of length \(h = 1\) mm from \(P\) in the directions of the axes, \(\vek a = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek b = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek c = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) (figure 2.232, left, the third fibre points towards the viewer), compute their vectors after loading exactly from the field (1.19), with no remainders left out, and compute the scalar triple product of these three vectors. The triple product divided by the volume \(h^3\) of the cube of fibres before loading is the ratio of the volumes. We denote it by \(r\). The right part of the figure shows the number \(r - 1\) against the fibre length \(h\), and the grey dashed horizontal line is at the height \(J - 1\). At \(h = 1\) mm we get \(r = 1 + 7{,}80603 \cdot 10^{-7}\), which differs from \(J\) by \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-10}\). For fibres of length \(0{,}1\) mm the difference is \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-11}\), ten times smaller. The difference is proportional to the length of the fibres, so the points in the figure lie on a straight line. The reason is that the remainders of this field are proportional to the square of the length of the step, as we saw in section 1.15. A remainder divided by the fibre length \(h\) is therefore proportional to \(h\), and each column of the determinant differs from the column without its remainder by that relative amount. When we shorten the fibres, the ratio of the volumes approaches \(J\). In general, however, we have shown this here only for this example. The sources do the same as we do: CM replaces the fibres by the vectors \(\mat F\) times the fibres and leaves the remainders out (CM (3.3.18), PDF p. 125). The exact claim needs two things. First, the volume of a body with curved faces, such as the true piece after loading, which exact adding up over the body gives. Second, the rule for how such adding up changes when we describe the points of the body by other variables, and in this rule exactly the Jacobian appears (KREYSZIG §10.3, PDF pp. 455-456, for areas). We develop both in chapter 4, where in section 4.3.5 we prove that the ratio of the volumes of the true piece after and before loading approaches \(J\) for every piece that shrinks to the point \(P\), not only for the parallelepiped of the fibres.

What sign does \(J\) have? Before loading \(\mat H\) is the zero matrix, \(\mat F = \mat I\) and \(J = 1\). If \(J\) were \(0\), then by lemma 2.75 on a zero determinant there would be a nonzero vector \(\vek v\) with \(\mat F\vek v = \vek 0\). A short fibre in the direction \(\vek v\) would then shrink to its remainder, which is small compared with its length, and the piece would be flattened, like the middle piece in the top row of figure 2.233 below, which is squeezed into a segment. But matter cannot be squeezed into nothing: the piece has mass, and this mass would end up in zero volume. CM therefore excludes \(J = 0\) as physically not realistic (CM, PDF pp. 119-120). If \(J\) were negative, the triple of fibres would change its orientation and the piece would become a mirror image of itself, in general also stretched. Such a deformation is described, for example, by the displacement field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -2x\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The point with the coordinates \((x, y, z)\) moves to the point \((x - 2x, y, z) = (-x, y, z)\), its mirror image in the plane \(x = 0\). The only nonzero partial derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = -2\), so the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) has the numbers \(1 - 2 = -1\), \(1\) and \(1\) on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, and by (2.70) \(J = (-1) \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = -1\). This field changes no distance. The differences of the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) of two points stay the same, and the difference of their coordinates \(x\) only changes sign, \((-x_1) - (-x_2) = -(x_1 - x_2)\), so its square stays the same. By definition 1.17 the distance between two points is the square root of the sum of these squares. So no fibre shrinks to nothing. Why then do we not count such a deformation as possible?

The answer lies in how the body reaches its final shape. We apply the load gradually, and the body passes through intermediate shapes (CM §3.2.1, PDF p. 111). For the mirror image the simplest way to imagine them is to multiply the displacements by a number \(t\) between \(0\) and \(1\): \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -2t\,x\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). At \(t = 0\) nothing moves, at \(t = 1\) we get the mirror image, and the values of \(t\) in between give the intermediate shapes. The deformation gradient has the numbers \(1 - 2t\), \(1\) and \(1\) on the diagonal, so on this path

\[J(t) = 1 - 2t .\]

At \(t = \tfrac12\) we have \(J = 0\). Then the point \((x, y, z)\) moves to \((x - x, y, z) = (0, y, z)\), and the whole body is squeezed into the plane \(x = 0\) (figure 2.233, top). On this path the body would have to be flattened before it is mirrored, and matter cannot do that.

Can we avoid the flattening if we go to the mirror image along another path? Let us add to the path two terms that are zero at the start and at the end:

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = -2t\,x + 2t(1 - t)\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = -2t(1 - t)\,x , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 .\]

At \(t = 0\) we have \(2t(1 - t) = 0\), and at \(t = 1\) as well, because then \(1 - t = 0\). So the path starts in the shape before loading and ends in the same mirror image as the first one. The deformation gradient is

\[\mat F(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 2t & 2t(1 - t) & 0 \\ -2t(1 - t) & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Of the six terms of (2.70) only the first, \(F_{\mathrm{xx}} F_{\mathrm{yy}} F_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1 - 2t\), and the fifth, \(-F_{\mathrm{xy}} F_{\mathrm{yx}} F_{\mathrm{zz}} = -2t(1 - t) \cdot \big(-2t(1 - t)\big) = 4t^2(1 - t)^2\), are nonzero. Each of the other four terms contains \(F_{\mathrm{xz}}\) or \(F_{\mathrm{yz}}\), which are zero. So on this path

\[J(t) = 1 - 2t + 4t^2(1 - t)^2 . \tag{2.76}\]

At \(t = \tfrac12\) we now have \(J = 0 + 4 \cdot \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac14 = 0{,}25\), and the piece is still a proper parallelogram (figure 2.233, bottom). At \(t = 1\), however, \(J = 1 - 2 + 0 = -1\). The graph in figure 2.234 shows that this \(J\) also passes through zero, somewhere near \(t = 0{,}61\). We cannot read this place off the formula (2.76), since we would have to solve an equation of the fourth degree.

We would like the conclusion the graph suggests for every path, not only for these two. It reads: a function that changes without jumps and is positive at the start and negative at the end is equal to zero somewhere in between. In the figure it looks self-evident, but it is not.

The function \(f(x) = x^2 - 3\) is a polynomial, so by corollary 1.65 on the sum and product of continuous functions, item 2, it is continuous. We have \(f(1) = -2 < 0\) and \(f(2) = 1 > 0\), but between \(1\) and \(2\) the function \(f\) is zero only at the point \(\sqrt 3\) (figure 2.235). No rational number has square 3 (lemma 1.28), so \(\sqrt 3\) is not a fraction. If we knew only fractions, the axis would hold only the dots of fractions, and at each of them the value of \(f\) is negative or positive, for example \(f(13/8) = -23/64\) and \(f(7/4) = 1/16\). This function would go from a negative value to a positive one through the hole in the axis without being equal to zero anywhere. So the conclusion depends on the number line having no holes, and we must prove it.

We have in fact already seen the proof. A number \(c\) with \(f(c) = 0\) is called a zero (ničla) of the function \(f\). Bisection in section 1.10.1 searched for exactly the zero of the function \(f(x) = x^2 - 3\). The rule kept the right half when \(m_{\mathrm{k}}^2 < 3\), that is, \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0\), and the left half when \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}}) \ge 0\). The first property of bisection, \(a_{\mathrm{k}}^2 < 3 \le b_{\mathrm{k}}^2\), says \(f(a_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0 \le f(b_{\mathrm{k}})\). We can use the same rule for every continuous function that is negative at the left endpoint and positive at the right one. The left endpoints then converge by the monotone convergence theorem 1.52, and the right ones converge to the same limit, because the lengths of the intervals are halved. Continuity then carries the inequalities \(f(a_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0\) and \(f(b_{\mathrm{k}}) \ge 0\) over to the limit.

Lemma 2.78 Zero of a continuous function (ničla zvezne funkcije)

Let \(a < b\) be real numbers and \(f\) a function whose input is a number \(x\) from the closed interval \([a, b]\) and whose output is a number \(f(x)\), and let \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\). If \(f(a) < 0 < f(b)\), there is a number \(c\) in the open interval \((a, b)\) with \(f(c) = 0\).

Proof

We must show that \(f\) has a zero strictly between \(a\) and \(b\). We find it by bisection, just as \(\sqrt 3\) in section 1.10.1. Every step of the proof is drawn on the example in figure 2.237 below, where \(f = -J\): the intervals \([a_{\mathrm{k}}, b_{\mathrm{k}}]\) are the rows, each below the previous one, the endpoints are the dots on the graph, and all intervals enclose the zero \(c\).

Building the intervals. We build the intervals \([a_{\mathrm{k}}, b_{\mathrm{k}}]\) step by step, so that at every \(k\) two requirements hold. The first: \(a \le a_{\mathrm{k}} < b_{\mathrm{k}} \le b\). The second: \(f(a_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0 \le f(b_{\mathrm{k}})\).

  1. Basis. Let \(a_1 = a\) and \(b_1 = b\). The first requirement holds because \(a < b\), the second because \(f(a) < 0\) and \(f(b) > 0\).
  2. For some \(k\) let \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}}\) be already determined so that both requirements hold, and let \(m_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(a_{\mathrm{k}} + b_{\mathrm{k}})\) be the midpoint of the interval. The midpoint lies strictly between the endpoints (section 1.10.1), so by the first requirement \(a < m_{\mathrm{k}} < b\), and the value \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}})\) is defined.
  3. If \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0\), let \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = m_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} = b_{\mathrm{k}}\). Otherwise \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}}) \ge 0\), and let \(a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} = m_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  4. In both cases both requirements also hold for \([a_{\mathrm{k}+1}, b_{\mathrm{k}+1}]\). The new endpoints are two of the numbers \(a_{\mathrm{k}} < m_{\mathrm{k}} < b_{\mathrm{k}}\), which all lie in \([a, b]\), and the left one is smaller than the right one. The new left endpoint is \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) or the midpoint with \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0\), and the new right endpoint is \(b_{\mathrm{k}}\) or the midpoint with \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}}) \ge 0\).
  5. Step 1 is the basis, and steps 2 to 4 are the induction step. So by the principle of induction 1.45, \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}}\) are determined for every natural number \(k\), and both requirements hold at every \(k\).

Properties.

  1. The left endpoints do not decrease and the right ones do not increase, \(a_{\mathrm{k}} \le a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le b_{\mathrm{k}}\), because a new endpoint is an old endpoint or the midpoint \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\), which lies between the old endpoints.
  2. The length of the interval is \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = (b - a)/2^{k-1}\). At \(k = 1\) this is \(b - a = (b - a)/2^0\). Every step halves the length, because each half has the length \(m_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}} = b_{\mathrm{k}} - m_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}})\). So the formula at \(k\) gives the formula at \(k + 1\), and by the principle of induction the formula holds for every \(k\), just as in step 11 of the proof of the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem 1.58.

The limit.

  1. The sequence of left endpoints \((a_{\mathrm{k}})\) is increasing by step 6 and bounded by the first requirement, since all its terms lie in \([a, b]\). So by the monotone convergence theorem 1.52 it converges to the number \(c = \sup\{a_{\mathrm{k}} : k \in \mathbb N\}\).
  2. By the first requirement \(a \le a_{\mathrm{k}} \le b\) for every \(k\), so by lemma 1.49 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 2, also \(a \le c \le b\). So the function \(f\) is defined and continuous at \(c\).
  3. By step 7 the right endpoints are \(b_{\mathrm{k}} = a_{\mathrm{k}} + (b - a) \cdot 1/2^{k-1}\). The sequence \((1/2^{k-1})\) converges to \(0\) by corollary 1.48 on the limit of the powers of one half. So by lemma 1.61 on limit laws for sequences, item 2, the sequence \(\big((b - a)/2^{k-1}\big)\) converges to \((b - a) \cdot 0 = 0\), and by item 1 of the same lemma the sequence \((b_{\mathrm{k}})\) converges to \(c + 0 = c\).
  4. The terms of both sequences of endpoints lie in \([a, b]\), and both sequences converge to \(c\). So by lemma 1.62 on continuity through sequences, first direction, the sequences \(\big(f(a_{\mathrm{k}})\big)\) and \(\big(f(b_{\mathrm{k}})\big)\) converge to \(f(c)\).
  5. By the second requirement \(f(a_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0\), so also \(f(a_{\mathrm{k}}) \le 0\), for every \(k\). The constant sequence \(0, 0, 0, \dots\) converges to \(0\) (section 1.9.2). So by lemma 1.49 that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 1, \(f(c) \le 0\).
  6. By the second requirement \(0 \le f(b_{\mathrm{k}})\) for every \(k\). By the same item of the lemma, with the constant sequence \(0, 0, 0, \dots\) on the left side of the inequality, \(0 \le f(c)\).
  7. By steps 12 and 13, \(f(c) = 0\).
  8. Since \(f(c) = 0\), \(f(a) < 0\) and \(f(b) > 0\), the number \(c\) is neither \(a\) nor \(b\). So by step 9 \(a < c < b\), that is, \(c \in (a, b)\).

Source: LEBL1 Lemma 3.3.7 (PDF pp. 132-133), with the same rule for the halves. The source shows that the two sequences of endpoints have the same limit by computing the limit of the difference \(b_{\mathrm{n}} - a_{\mathrm{n}}\) as \(\lim 2^{1-n}(b - a) = 0\). We write the right endpoints through the left ones and the length of the interval and use the limit laws for sequences.

The proof repeated bisection for \(\sqrt 3\) from section 1.10.1, except that instead of the square of the midpoint it looks at the sign of the value \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}})\). The number \(c\) was supplied by the completeness axiom, hidden in the monotone convergence theorem, as for the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem 1.58. That the length of the interval goes to zero is the corollary on the limit of the powers of one half, which rests on the Archimedean property 1.36 through lemma 1.40 on the limit of the sequence 1/n. We needed continuity in step 11, where we concluded from the convergence of the endpoints that the values converge. The strict inequality \(f(a_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0\) turned in step 12 into the non-strict \(f(c) \le 0\), because a limit preserves only non-strict inequalities. So the left endpoints give only \(f(c) \le 0\), the right ones \(f(c) \ge 0\), and only both inequalities together give \(f(c) = 0\). And what if at some \(k\) the value \(f(m_{\mathrm{k}})\) is exactly zero? Then we have already found the zero. The rule does not check for this separately. It keeps the left half, which has \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) as its right endpoint, and the proof goes on unchanged.

The lemma speaks only about the value \(0\) and only about a function that is negative at the left endpoint. The Jacobian on our paths, however, is positive at the start, and in general we are interested in any value between the values at the endpoints. We get both extensions by subtracting a number from the function or the function from a number.

Theorem 2.79 Intermediate value theorem (izrek o vmesni vrednosti)

Let \(a < b\) be real numbers and \(f\) a function whose input is a number \(x\) from the closed interval \([a, b]\) and whose output is a number \(f(x)\), and let \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\). If \(y\) is a number with \(f(a) < y < f(b)\) or \(f(a) > y > f(b)\), there is a number \(c\) in the open interval \((a, b)\) with \(f(c) = y\).

Proof

We must show that \(f\) takes the value \(y\) strictly between \(a\) and \(b\). In both cases we build a function \(g\) that is negative at \(a\), positive at \(b\) and zero exactly where \(f\) equals \(y\), and we use the lemma on the zero of a continuous function.

1. The case \(f(a) < y < f(b)\).

  1. Let \(g(x) = f(x) + (-y)\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\).
  2. The constant function with the value \(-y\) is continuous at every point, because \(|(-y) - (-y)| = 0 < \eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\) and every \(x\), so every band \(\delta\) will do. So by corollary 1.65 on the sum and product of continuous functions, item 1, the sum \(g\) is continuous at every point of the interval \([a, b]\).
  3. We have \(g(a) = f(a) - y < 0\) and \(g(b) = f(b) - y > 0\).
  4. By lemma 2.78 on the zero of a continuous function there is \(c \in (a, b)\) with \(g(c) = 0\). Then \(f(c) - y = 0\), that is, \(f(c) = y\).

2. The case \(f(a) > y > f(b)\).

  1. Let \(g(x) = y + (-1) \cdot f(x)\) for every \(x \in [a, b]\).
  2. By corollary 1.65 on the sum and product of continuous functions, item 1, the multiple \((-1) \cdot f\) is continuous at every point of the interval \([a, b]\). The constant function with the value \(y\) is continuous as in step 2 of the first case, so by the same item of the corollary the sum \(g\) is continuous.
  3. We have \(g(a) = y - f(a) < 0\) and \(g(b) = y - f(b) > 0\).
  4. By lemma 2.78 on the zero of a continuous function there is \(c \in (a, b)\) with \(g(c) = 0\). Then \(y - f(c) = 0\), that is, \(f(c) = y\).

Source: LEBL1 Thm 3.3.8 (PDF p. 133), where it is called Bolzano's intermediate value theorem, with the same proof.

The theorem says that a function without jumps cannot skip any intermediate value on its way from \(f(a)\) to \(f(b)\) (figure 2.236, left). It says only that such a \(c\) exists, not how many there are. In the figure the equation \(f(c) = y\) has three solutions, \(c_1\), \(c_2\) and \(c_3\), and the proof of the lemma finds only one of them.

Continuity is needed. Take the steel bar of length 10 m from section 1.12.2, which hangs under its own weight and has at the depth 5 m a pin with two weights that together weigh 20 N. The force \(S(x)\) with which the cross section at the depth \(x\) carries everything below it falls from \(S(0) = 80{,}10\) N at the top to \(S(10\ \text{m}) = 0\) at the lower end. But it takes the value \(40\) N, which lies in between, nowhere (figure 2.236, right). Above the pin \(S(x) \ge 50{,}05\) N by (1.28), below it \(S(x) < 30{,}05\) N, and at 5 m the function jumps over all values between them. The completeness axiom is needed too, as the function \(x^2 - 3\) showed, which has no zero among the fractions.

Let us return to the second path to the mirror image. Its Jacobian \(J(t) = 1 - 2t + 4t^2(1 - t)^2\) from (2.76) is a polynomial in the variable \(t\), so by corollary 1.65 on the sum and product of continuous functions, item 2, it is continuous on the interval \([0, 1]\). We have \(J(0) = 1 > 0 > -1 = J(1)\). So by the intermediate value theorem with \(y = 0\), which lies between \(J(0)\) and \(J(1)\), there is \(c \in (0, 1)\) with \(J(c) = 0\), and this without solving an equation of the fourth degree. Since the value at the left endpoint is larger than \(y = 0\), the proof of the theorem used the lemma on the zero of a continuous function on the function \(g(t) = 0 - J(t) = -J(t)\). Bisection for \(g\) keeps the right half when \(g(m_{\mathrm{k}}) < 0\), that is, \(J(m_{\mathrm{k}}) > 0\), and the left half when \(J(m_{\mathrm{k}}) \le 0\). The table shows the first eight steps, and figure 2.237 the first five intervals.

\(k\) \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(b_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(b_{\mathrm{k}} - a_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(m_{\mathrm{k}}\) \(J(m_{\mathrm{k}})\) next interval
1 0 1 1 0,5 \(0{,}25\) right half
2 0,5 1 0,5 0,75 \(-0{,}359375\) left half
3 0,5 0,75 0,25 0,625 \(-0{,}0302\dots\) left half
4 0,5 0,625 0,125 0,5625 \(0{,}1172\dots\) right half
5 0,5625 0,625 0,0625 0,59375 \(0{,}0452\dots\) right half
6 0,59375 0,625 0,03125 0,609375 \(0{,}0078\dots\) right half
7 0,609375 0,625 0,015625 0,6171875 \(-0{,}0110\dots\) left half
8 0,609375 0,6171875 0,0078125 0,61328125 \(-0{,}0015\dots\) left half

The endpoints and midpoints are fractions with the denominators \(1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\) and are written exactly. The values \(J(m_{\mathrm{k}})\) that end with three dots are cut off after four decimals, the others are exact. The left endpoints increase towards \(c\) and the right ones decrease towards \(c\), so \(c\) lies in every interval. After eight steps \(c\) therefore lies in the left half of the eighth interval, between \(0{,}609375\) and \(0{,}61328125\). The twentieth interval \([a_{20}, b_{20}]\) has the length \(1/2^{19}\), less than \(2 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and the endpoints \(0{,}6126346\dots\) and \(0{,}6126365\dots\), so \(c = 0{,}61263\dots\) Since \(J(c) = 0\), by lemma 2.75 on a zero determinant there is a nonzero vector \(\vek v\) with \(\mat F(c)\,\vek v = \vek 0\). The third row of the matrix \(\mat F(c)\) gives \(v_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), the second \(-2c(1 - c)\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + v_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\). So for \(v_{\mathrm{x}} = 1\) we get \(v_{\mathrm{y}} = 2c(1 - c) = 0{,}4746\dots\), and the first row gives \((1 - 2c)\,v_{\mathrm{x}} + 2c(1 - c)\,v_{\mathrm{y}} = \big(1 - 2c + 4c^2(1 - c)^2\big)\,v_{\mathrm{x}} = J(c)\,v_{\mathrm{x}} = 0\), as it must. At \(t = c\) the fibre in the direction of the vector \(\vek v\) shrinks to nothing, and the piece is flattened into a segment (figure 2.233, bottom).

Now we can state the conclusion about the sign of \(J\) precisely. First let us say what we assume about the loading.

  1. Loading parameter. We describe the loading by a number \(t\) from the interval \([0, 1]\), which we call the loading parameter (parameter obremenitve). At \(t = 0\) the body is before loading, at \(t = 1\) in the final state, and the values of \(t\) in between correspond to the intermediate states. We may think of \(t\) as the fraction of the loading time that has already passed. CM describes a body loaded slowly in this way: it occupies one intermediate shape after another, and CM calls the shape at the time \(t\) a configuration (CM §3.2.1, PDF p. 111).
  2. A displacement field for every \(t\). For every \(t\) the body has a continuously differentiable displacement field (definition 1.91), measured from the shape before loading, and \(P\) is an interior point of the body. We write \(\mat H(t)\) for the displacement gradient at \(P\) at this \(t\), \(\mat F(t) = \mat I + \mat H(t)\) for the deformation gradient, and \(J(t) = \det\mat F(t)\) for the Jacobian. Before loading nothing moves, so \(\mat H(0) = \mat 0\).
  3. No jumps. Each of the nine entries \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\), the partial derivative \(\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) at the point \(P\) at the parameter \(t\), is a continuous function of the variable \(t\) on \([0, 1]\) (definition 1.59 of continuity). This is an idealization of gradual loading: the shape of the piece at \(P\) does not change in an instant. Assumptions 2 and 3 fail if the body tears at \(P\). Without the third assumption the conclusion fails: \(J\) could jump from \(1\) to \(-1\) without ever being zero in between, just as the force in the bar with the pin jumps over the value \(40\) N.
  4. Matter is not squeezed into nothing. At no \(t\) is \(J(t) = 0\). Every intermediate state is a shape of the same body, so the argument by which we excluded \(J = 0\) above holds for it: the piece at \(P\) would be flattened (CM, PDF pp. 119-120). This is the assumption that excludes the mirror image, as we shall see after the corollary.
Corollary 2.80 Positive Jacobian (pozitivna Jacobijeva determinanta)

For every number \(t\) from the interval \([0, 1]\) let a \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat H(t)\) be given whose entries \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\) are continuous functions of the variable \(t\) on \([0, 1]\). Let \(\mat H(0) = \mat 0\), and let \(J(t) = \det\big(\mat I + \mat H(t)\big) \neq 0\) for every \(t \in [0, 1]\). Then \(J(t) > 0\) for every \(t \in [0, 1]\).

Proof

We must show that \(J\) is negative at no point of the interval \([0, 1]\). We argue by contradiction, with the intermediate value theorem.

  1. The entries of the matrix \(\mat F(t) = \mat I + \mat H(t)\) are \(F_{\mathrm{ij}}(t) = 1 + H_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\) for \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{ij}}(t) = H_{\mathrm{ij}}(t)\) for \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\). The constant function with the value \(1\) is continuous at every point, because \(|1 - 1| = 0 < \eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\). So by corollary 1.65 on the sum and product of continuous functions, item 1, all entries \(F_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are continuous on \([0, 1]\).
  2. By (2.70), \(J(t)\) is the sum of six products of three entries of the matrix \(\mat F(t)\) each, three of which are multiplied by \(-1\). A product of three functions is a product of two, multiplied by the third. So by item 1 of the same corollary, applied to each product, multiple and sum separately, \(J\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\).
  3. Since \(\mat H(0) = \mat 0\), we have \(\mat F(0) = \mat I\) and \(J(0) = \det\mat I = 1\). By (2.70), for the matrix \(\mat I\) only the first term, \(1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1\), is nonzero, because every other term contains an entry off the diagonal, which is zero.
  4. Suppose that \(J(s) < 0\) for some \(s \in [0, 1]\). Since \(J(0) = 1\), we have \(s \neq 0\), so \(s > 0\), and \([0, s]\) is an interval.
  5. The function \(J\) is continuous on \([0, s]\) too. The continuity condition (1.27) on the set \([0, s]\) checks only some of the points that it checks on \([0, 1]\), so the same band \(\delta\) will do for it.
  6. We have \(J(0) = 1 > 0 > J(s)\). By the intermediate value theorem 2.79 on the interval \([0, s]\), with the value \(y = 0\), which lies between \(J(0)\) and \(J(s)\), there is \(c \in (0, s)\) with \(J(c) = 0\). In the same way each graph in figure 2.234, which starts at \(J = 1\) and ends below zero, crosses the horizontal axis.
  7. The number \(c\) lies in \([0, 1]\), so by the hypothesis \(J(c) \neq 0\). This contradicts step 6, so the supposition of step 4 is false.
  8. So \(J(t) \ge 0\) for every \(t \in [0, 1]\), and since \(J(t) \neq 0\) by the hypothesis, \(J(t) > 0\).

Source: The corollary and its proof are not from the sources. CM assumes that the Jacobian is positive (CM, PDF p. 126), BOWER requires it for every physically possible displacement field (BOWER §2.1.4, PDF p. 47).

Assumptions 1 to 4 give exactly the hypotheses of the corollary. So \(J(t) > 0\) at every \(t\), in particular in the final state at \(t = 1\). Both paths to the mirror image violate the fourth assumption, the first at \(t = \tfrac12\), the second at \(t = c\), and the corollary says that every path without jumps (assumptions 2 and 3) that ends at \(J < 0\) would violate it. CM and BOWER only require the Jacobian to be positive. CM assumes it so that the orientation of the fibres is preserved (CM, PDF p. 126), and BOWER says that it must hold for every physically possible displacement field, because matter cannot disappear (BOWER §2.1.4, PDF p. 47). The corollary shows that for gradual loading the requirement that matter is not squeezed into nothing is enough. The mirror image need not be excluded separately.

For \(J > 0\) the parallelepiped after loading has \(J\) times the volume it had before. The volume grows if \(J > 1\) and shrinks if \(J < 1\). For \(J = 1\) it does not change. In section 1.6.2 we called such a deformation isochoric (CM §3.3.2.1, PDF p. 122).

There remains the relation with strains. By (1.59) the diagonal entries of the small strain tensor are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{xx}}) = H_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = H_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = H_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The sum \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) in item 2 of the lemma is therefore \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), the trace of the small strain tensor from section 1.17. For small partial derivatives therefore

\[J - 1 \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} ,\]

with an error of at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3\), where \(g\) is the largest absolute value of the nine partial derivatives of the displacements. For \(g = 0{,}001\) this is at most \(6{,}006 \cdot 10^{-6}\). The normal strains are at most \(g\) in absolute value, and the error is smaller by about a factor \(6g\), just as for the sheared cube the term with the square of the shift was smaller than the term with the shift itself by a factor of the ratio of the shift to the height. This is the relation we announced in section 1.17, now with a derivation and with a bound for the error (BOWER §2.1.9, PDF p. 51). When all partial derivatives of the displacements are small, the relative change of volume of a small piece is approximately the sum of the normal strains. The entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) off the diagonal, from which the shear strains are built, appear only in the second bracket of (2.75) and in \(\det\mat H\), so they change the volume only by terms of size \(g^2\) and \(g^3\). We can see why: in the sheared cube the top face slides sideways, while the height above the table stays the same.

Let us test this on all three stories we know.

The sheared cube. A steel cube with the edge 10 mm is glued to a table by its bottom face, and we pushed its top face by 10 µm in the direction of the axis \(x\), with the axis \(z\) pointing up. The displacement field was \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) ((1.17)). The only nonzero partial derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = 0{,}001\), so \(\mat F\) has ones on the diagonal, the number \(0{,}001\) at the place \(xz\), and zeros elsewhere. Of the six terms of (2.70) only the product of the diagonal entries is nonzero. Every other term contains at least one entry below the diagonal, at the place \(yx\), \(zx\) or \(zy\), and these are all zero. So \(J = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1 = 1\), exactly, not only approximately. The same holds for every push, even a large one, since the number \(0{,}001\) does not appear in \(J\) at all. The column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat F\) is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} + 0{,}001\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), so a multiple of the column \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) has been added to the column \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). As in figure 2.218, where the top face moves parallel to the base and the height stays the same, this does not change the determinant: \(\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}} + 0{,}001\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = \det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}) + 0{,}001\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) = 1 + 0\). The approximation agrees too: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\). Simple shear is isochoric, as CM also says for the same kind of example (CM Example 3.3.1, PDF pp. 120 and 122, CM (3.3.15), PDF p. 124).

The hanging bar. At the point \(P\) the sum of the normal strains is

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2 \cdot 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

and the exact value is \(J - 1 = 7{,}80798 \cdot 10^{-7}\). The difference is \(1{,}9 \cdot 10^{-12}\), four hundred thousand times less than the change itself. So the volume of a piece at \(P\) grows by \(7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\) of its value. Why exactly \(7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\), which is \(0{,}4\) times the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) along the bar? The piece gets longer along the bar by the fraction \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and across the bar it shrinks in both directions by \(0{,}3\) times this fraction, because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (figure 2.238). So its volume is multiplied by

\[(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})(1 - 0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})(1 - 0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}) \approx 1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - 0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - 0{,}3\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1 + 0{,}4\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} ,\]

where we left out the products of two or three strains. The exact product is \(1 + 0{,}4\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - 0{,}51\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + 0{,}09\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^3\), and at \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) the two terms left out add up to \(-1{,}94 \cdot 10^{-12}\), which is the difference between the approximation and the exact value above. The lengthening along the bar is larger than the total shrinking across it, so the volume of steel in a bar under tension grows a little. This holds as long as the field (1.19) holds, that is, far from the place where a real ceiling holds the bar, and as long as the steel does not deform permanently.

A rigid rotation. In section 1.17 we turned a thin square plate lying in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) as a whole about the axis \(z\), without deforming it. The rotation was given by the pair \(c = 0{,}6\), \(s = 0{,}8\) (here \(c\) is not the zero from above but the number from section 1.17), for which \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\). The fibre \(OA\) of length \(5\) has after the rotation the component \(5c = 3\) along the axis \(x\) and the component \(5s = 4\) along the axis \(y\). The displacement field was \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = (c - 1)\,x - s\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = s\,x + (c - 1)\,y\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), and the deformation gradient

\[\mat F = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

By (2.70), \(J = 0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}6 \cdot 1 - (-0{,}8) \cdot 0{,}8 \cdot 1 = 0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). A rigid rotation does not change the volume, as it must not, since it changes no distance. But the sum of the normal strains is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = (c - 1) + (c - 1) + 0 = -0{,}8\). The term \(c - 1 = -0{,}4\) is the shortening of the component of the fibre \(OA\) from \(5\) to \(3\), divided by \(5\), although the fibre itself has kept the length \(5\). The approximation would predict that the volume shrinks by \(80\) %, which is wrong. Here the partial derivatives are not small, since \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = -0{,}8\), and the error bound \(6g^2 + 6g^3\) with \(g = 0{,}8\) is not small. In (2.75) the second bracket, which is \(0{,}8\), exactly cancels the first, and \(\det\mat H\) is zero. So the relation \(J - 1 \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) holds only when all partial derivatives of the displacements are small, also those that describe a rotation. The exact formula \(J = \det\mat F\) holds always.

The determinant has given us three tools. It tells whether a matrix sends some nonzero vector to zero, which we proved with the columns and the rows as edges of parallelepipeds. It tells when a matrix has an inverse matrix, and it also computes the inverse from the vector products of the columns. It tells how many times the volume of a small piece of a body grows, for which we needed the rule for the determinant of a product. With it we can now look for faces on which the traction vector points along the normal. In pure shear we saw that for such a face \(\det(\ten\sigma - \tau_0\,\mat I) = 0\). In the next section we will find, for any stress matrix, all numbers \(\lambda\) with \(\det(\ten\sigma - \lambda\,\mat I) = 0\), and the faces that belong to them.
